stem: A company has millions of objects in an Amazon S3 bucket. The objects are in the S3 Standard storage class. All the S3 objects are accessed frequently. The number of users and applications that access the objects is increasing rapidly. The objects are encrypted with server-side encryption with AWS KMS Keys (SSE-KMS). A solutions architect reviews the company's monthly AWS invoice and notices that AWS KMS costs are increasing because of the high number of requests from Amazon S3. The solutions architect needs to optimize costs with minimal changes to the application. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Create a new S3 bucket that has server-side encryption with customer-provided keys (SSE-C) as the encryption type. Copy the existing objects to the new S3 bucket. Specify SSE-C.

Create a new S3 bucket that has server-side encryption with Amazon S3 managed keys (SSE-S3) as the encryption type. Use S3 Batch Operations to copy the existing objects to the new S3 bucket. Specify SSE-S3.
Use AWS CloudHSM to store the encryption keys. Create a new S3 bucket. Use S3 Batch Operations to copy the existing objects to the new S3 bucket. Encrypt the objects by using the keys from CloudHSM.

Use the S3 Intelligent-Tiering storage class for the S3 bucket. Create an S3 Intelligent- Tiering archive configuration to transition objects that are not accessed for 90 days to S3 Glacier Deep Archive.

explanation:
SSE-S3 uses keys that Amazon S3 manages, so there is no per-request KMS charge and no extra latency. S3 Batch Operations can
copy all existing objects into a new SSE-S3 bucket without writing code. The application keeps using S3 the same way, so changes are
minimal.
wrongOptionsExplanation:
A. SSE-C makes the client send the key with every request. That adds work to every application and key management is entirely
yours, the opposite of low overhead. C. CloudHSM adds a dedicated HSM cluster to run and pay for. It would increase cost and
operations, not reduce them. D. Intelligent-Tiering and Deep Archive change storage cost, not KMS request cost. The data is accessed
frequently, so archiving it makes no sense.
plainWords:
Millions of frequently read objects use SSE-KMS, and every read or write makes a KMS API call that you pay for. You want to cut that
bill with the least work.
keyPoints:
• KMS charges per request; S3 with SSE-KMS makes many requests. • If you must keep SSE-KMS, enabling S3 Bucket Keys reduces
KMS calls by up to about 99 percent. If you do not need KMS control, SSE-S3 is the simplest fix.
Reference: AWS documentation — https://docs.aws.amazon.com/

stem: An ecommerce company runs an application on AWS. The application has an Amazon API Gateway API that invokes an AWS Lambda function. The data is stored in an Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL DB instance. During the company's most recent flash sale, a sudden increase in API calls negatively affected the application's performance. A solutions architect reviewed the Amazon CloudWatch metrics during that time and noticed a significant increase in Lambda invocations and database connections. The CPU utilization also was high on the DB instance. What should the solutions architect recommend to optimize the application's performance?

options.text: Increase the memory of the Lambda function. Modify the Lambda function to close the database connections when the data is retrieved.
Add an Amazon ElastiCache for Redis cluster to store the frequently accessed data from the RDS database.
Create an RDS proxy by using the Lambda console. Modify the Lambda function to use the proxy endpoint.
Modify the Lambda function to connect to the database outside of the function's handler. Check for an existing database connection before creating a new connection.

explanation:
RDS Proxy sits between Lambda and the database and pools and reuses connections. Thousands of short-lived Lambda invocations
share a small, steady set of real database connections. You create it from the Lambda console and just change the endpoint in the
function.
wrongOptionsExplanation:
A. More Lambda memory does not reduce connections. Closing connections after each call can make the churn worse and increases
connection setup cost. B. ElastiCache helps repeated reads but does not fix the connection explosion for writes and uncached
queries. It also needs application changes. D. Opening the connection outside the handler reuses it only inside one warm execution
environment. During a big spike there are many environments, so connections still multiply.
plainWords:
A flash sale makes Lambda scale out. Each concurrent Lambda opens its own database connection, so the PostgreSQL instance runs
out of connections and CPU.
keyPoints:
• Lambda + relational database + "too many connections" = RDS Proxy. • RDS Proxy also shortens failover time and can use IAM
authentication and Secrets Manager.
Reference: AWS documentation — https://docs.aws.amazon.com/

stem: A company is migrating an application to the AWS Cloud. The application runs in an on- premises data center and writes thousands of images into a mounted NFS file system each night. After the company migrates the application, the company will host the application on an Amazon EC2 instance with a mounted Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) file system. The company has established an AWS Direct Connect connection to AWS. Before the migration cutover, a solutions architect must build a process that will replicate the newly created on-premises images to the EFS file system. What is the MOST operationally efficient way to replicate the images?

options.text: Configure a periodic process to run the aws s3 sync command from the on-premises file system to Amazon S3. Configure an AWS Lambda function to process event notifications from Amazon S3 and copy the images from Amazon S3 to the EFS file system.

Deploy an AWS Storage Gateway file gateway with an NFS mount point. Mount the file gateway file system on the on-premises server. Configure a process to periodically copy the images to the mount point.

Deploy an AWS DataSync agent to an on-premises server that has access to the NFS file system. Send data over the Direct Connect connection to an S3 bucket by using public VIF. Configure an AWS Lambda function to process event notifications from Amazon S3 and copy the images from Amazon S3 to the EFS file system.

Deploy an AWS DataSync agent on premises with access to the NFS file system. Connect the agent privately to the AWS DataSync VPC service endpoint over Direct Connect using a private virtual interface. Schedule a DataSync task to transfer newly created images directly to the Amazon EFS file system every 24 hours.

explanation: D is correct after a necessary technical wording correction: the AWS PrivateLink VPC interface endpoint belongs to the DataSync service, not to Amazon EFS. The on-premises DataSync agent reads the NFS share; DataSync uses task network interfaces to write directly to EFS. A and C introduce unnecessary S3 staging and Lambda orchestration. B uses S3-backed File Gateway rather than directly replicating to EFS. The private Direct Connect virtual interface and routing support the DataSync VPC endpoint and data-plane interfaces. Original D retained in originalQuestionSnapshot.
wrongOptionsExplanation:
A. A custom s3 sync script plus S3 events plus a Lambda copy to EFS has many moving parts to build and monitor (and Lambda time
limits). B. A File Gateway stores data in S3, not EFS, so you would still need another step to move files into EFS. C. Sends data to S3
first and then needs Lambda to copy to EFS. It works but is far less efficient than copying straight to EFS.
plainWords:
Each night new images land on an on-prem NFS share. Before cutover they must be copied to Amazon EFS over an existing Direct
Connect link, with as little operational work as possible.
keyPoints:
• NFS/SMB to AWS storage on a schedule = DataSync. DataSync can target EFS, FSx and S3 directly. • Use a DataSync VPC
(interface) endpoint to keep transfers private over Direct Connect.
HEADS-UP ON THIS QUESTION
• Option D has been restored from matching online exam-question copies. The intended design is DataSync agent -> DataSync PrivateLink interface endpoint -> EFS. The source wording incorrectly calls it an endpoint for Amazon EFS.
Reference: AWS documentation — https://docs.aws.amazon.com/
SOURCE WARNING: Option D restored from third-party copies; technical wording caveat remains.
sourceWarning: Option D was truncated in the original source PDF. Full option restored from matching third-party exam question text; wording refers to a PrivateLink endpoint for Amazon EFS, but technically the interface VPC endpoint is for AWS DataSync. Answer key D is source-reported, not independently certified by AWS.

review.restoration: Option D completed from matching online question copies
review.technicalCaveat: Source option D incorrectly describes an interface VPC endpoint for EFS; corrected to DataSync VPC service endpoint.

stem: A solutions architect has launched multiple Amazon EC2 instances in a placement group within a single Availability Zone. Because of additional load on the system, the solutions architect attempts to add new instances to the placement group. However, the solutions architect receives an insufficient capacity error. What should the solutions architect do to troubleshoot this issue?

options.text: Use a spread placement group. Set a minimum of eight instances for each Availability Zone.
Stop and start all the instances in the placement group. Try the launch again.
Create a new placement group. Merge the new placement group with the original placement group.
Launch the additional instances as Dedicated Hosts in the placement groups.

explanation:
A cluster placement group needs capacity on closely grouped hardware. If the original hardware cannot fit more, stopping and
starting all the instances in the group lets AWS re-place them together on hardware with enough room, and then the new launch can
succeed. AWS also recommends launching all needed instances in one request and using the same instance type.
wrongOptionsExplanation:
A. A spread placement group has a different purpose (separate hardware) and supports at most 7 running instances per AZ. It does
not solve a capacity error. C. You cannot merge placement groups. D. Dedicated Hosts cannot be launched into a placement group,
and they do not fix capacity.
plainWords: Instances live in a cluster placement group in one Availability Zone. Adding more fails with an insufficient capacity error.
keyPoints:
• Capacity error in a cluster placement group: stop and start all instances (or relaunch them together) and retry. • Cluster = low
latency (one AZ). Spread = isolation. Partition = large distributed systems.
Reference: AWS documentation — https://docs.aws.amazon.com/

stem: A VPC spans three Availability Zones, each with public and private subnets. One NAT gateway and one internet gateway exist. Private EC2 instances must connect to the internet.

options.text: Add two more NAT gateways (one per AZ). Configure each private subnet to use its AZ’s NAT gateway.
Add two more NAT gateways and configure public subnets.
Add internet gateways per AZ and route private subnets.
Add internet gateways per AZ and configure public subnets.

explanation:
A NAT gateway lives in one AZ. If that AZ fails, every private subnet using it loses internet access. Creating one NAT gateway in a
public subnet in each AZ, and routing each private subnet to the NAT gateway in its own AZ, gives AZ-level resilience and avoids
cross-AZ data charges.
wrongOptionsExplanation:
B. Adds NAT gateways but does not point the private subnets at them, so nothing changes. C. You attach only one internet gateway
per VPC, and it is already there. Private subnets need NAT, not more IGWs. D. Same problem as C: extra internet gateways are not
possible and do not give private instances outbound-only access.
plainWords: A VPC has three AZs but only one NAT gateway. Private instances in all AZs depend on it.
keyPoints:
• One NAT gateway per AZ, each private route table points to the NAT in the same AZ. • NAT gateways are zonal; the internet
gateway is regional and redundant by design.
Reference: AWS documentation — https://docs.aws.amazon.com/

stem: A multi-tenant software as a service (SaaS) customer support platform serves thousands of enterprise clients. The platform must deploy more than 5,000 customized models that use the same ML framework to classify tickets, optimize inference infrastructure costs, and maintain sub-200 ms latency. The platform must operate in a multiaccount AWS architecture that includes separate accounts for development, staging, and production environments. Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?

options.text: Deploy each model to a dedicated Amazon SageMaker AI real-time endpoint. Provision ml.g5.xlarge instances to handle peak traffic. Use cross-account IAM roles to grant AWS accounts access to model artifacts.
Deploy models by using Amazon SageMaker AI multi-model endpoints with inference components. Enable auto scaling in a centralized production account.

Deploy models to individual Amazon SageMaker AI serverless inference endpoints. Configure auto scaling. Deploy the endpoints in separate AWS accounts for each environment. Use cross-account Amazon S3 bucket policies to share models.
Deploy models to Amazon SageMaker AI asynchronous inference endpoints. Use Amazon S3 to queue requests from multiple accounts. Use batch transform jobs to perform offline processing.

explanation:
Multi-model endpoints (with inference components) host many models behind shared compute and load them on demand, which is
exactly the pattern for thousands of similar models. You pay for a pooled fleet instead of thousands of idle endpoints, and auto
scaling in the production account keeps latency under control.
wrongOptionsExplanation:
A. One dedicated real-time endpoint per model for 5,000 models is extremely expensive and idle most of the time. C. Thousands of
serverless endpoints create cold starts that threaten the 200 ms target and are hard to manage per account. D. Asynchronous
inference and batch transform are not designed for low-latency real-time responses.
plainWords:
A SaaS platform must serve more than 5,000 custom models that use the same ML framework, keep latency below 200 ms, and keep
inference cost low, across dev, staging and prod accounts.
keyPoints:
• Many models, same framework, cost-sensitive = multi-model endpoint. • Real-time latency requirement rules out async inference
and batch transform.
Reference: AWS documentation — https://docs.aws.amazon.com/

stem: A company operates an on-premises software-as-a-service (SaaS) solution that ingests several files daily. The company provides multiple public SFTP endpoints to its customers to facilitate the file transfers. The customers add the SFTP endpoint IP addresses to their firewall allow list for outbound traffic. Changes to the SFTP endmost IP addresses are not permitted. The company wants to migrate the SaaS solution to AWS and decrease the operational overhead of the file transfer service. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Register the customer-owned block of IP addresses in the company's AWS account. Create Elastic IP addresses from the address pool and assign them to an AWS Transfer for SFTP endpoint. Use AWS Transfer to store the files in Amazon S3.

Add a subnet containing the customer-owned block of IP addresses to a VPC Create Elastic IP addresses from the address pool and assign them to an Application Load Balancer (ALB). Launch EC2 instances hosting FTP services in an Auto Scaling group behind the ALB. Store the files in attached Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) volumes.

Register the customer-owned block of IP addresses with Amazon Route 53. Create alias records in Route 53 that point to a Network Load Balancer (NLB). Launch EC2 instances hosting FTP services in an Auto Scaling group behind the NLB. Store the files in Amazon S3.

Register the customer-owned block of IP addresses in the company's AWS account. Create Elastic IP addresses from the address pool and assign them to an Amazon S3 VPC endpoint. Enable SFTP support on the S3 bucket.

explanation: A is correct, provided the AWS Transfer Family SFTP server is configured with an internet-facing VPC-hosted endpoint. Transfer Family supports attaching Elastic IPs allocated from a customer-owned BYOIP prefix, preserving IPs already in clients' firewall allowlists. A public (non-VPC-hosted) Transfer Family endpoint does not support attaching static IPs. B incorrectly uses an ALB for SFTP/FTP and adds unmanaged EC2 servers; C uses NLB but still requires self-managed servers and the BYOIP registration is wrong; D cannot enable SFTP on an S3 VPC endpoint. Source key A retained.
wrongOptionsExplanation:
B. An ALB cannot be given Elastic IPs, and running FTP servers on EC2 with EBS is high effort. C. Route 53 does not register IP blocks,
and you would again manage EC2 FTP servers. D. S3 does not provide an SFTP endpoint, and VPC endpoints do not take Elastic IPs
this way.
plainWords:
Customers allow-list the SFTP server IP addresses. Those addresses cannot change after the move to AWS. You also want less
operational work.
keyPoints:
• Need SFTP/FTPS/FTP into S3 or EFS = AWS Transfer Family. • Must keep existing public IPs = BYOIP then assign EIPs.
Reference: AWS documentation — https://docs.aws.amazon.com/

stem: A company wants to use AWS for disaster recovery for an on-premises application. The company has hundreds of Windows-based servers that run the application. All the servers mount a common share. The company has an RTO of 15 minutes and an RPO of 5 minutes. The solution must support native failover and fallback capabilities. Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?

options.text: Create an AWS Storage Gateway File Gateway. Schedule daily Windows server backups. Save the data lo Amazon S3. During a disaster, recover the on-premises servers from the backup. During failback. run the on-premises servers on Amazon EC2 instances.

Create a set of AWS CloudFormation templates to create infrastructure. Replicate all data to Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) by using AWS DataSync. During a disaster, use AWS CodePipeline to deploy the templates to restore the on-premises servers. Fail back the data by using DataSync.

Create an AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK) pipeline to stand up a multi-site active-active environment on AWS. Replicate data into Amazon S3 by using the s3 sync command. During a disaster, swap DNS endpoints to point to AWS. Fail back the data by using the s3 sync command.

Use AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery to replicate the on-premises servers. Replicate data to an Amazon FSx for Windows File Server file system by using AWS DataSync. Mount the file system to AWS servers. During a disaster, fail over the on-premises servers to AWS. Fail back to new or existing servers by using Elastic Disaster Recovery.

explanation:
AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery continuously replicates servers at block level (RPO of seconds) and launches recovery instances in
minutes, and it includes a built-in failback process. Pairing it with Amazon FSx for Windows File Server (SMB, Active Directory aware)
and DataSync handles the shared Windows file share. Staging resources are small until a real failover, so it is cost effective.
wrongOptionsExplanation:
A. Daily backups cannot meet a 5-minute RPO or 15-minute RTO. B. Rebuilding with CloudFormation and CodePipeline after a disaster
takes far longer than 15 minutes and EFS is for Linux (NFS), not Windows shares. C. Active-active meets the goals but costs far more,
and s3 sync is not an SMB file share replacement.
plainWords:
Hundreds of on-prem Windows servers sharing a file share need DR to AWS with RTO 15 minutes, RPO 5 minutes, and native failover
and failback, as cheaply as possible.
keyPoints:
• RTO minutes + RPO seconds/minutes + servers = Elastic Disaster Recovery (continuous replication, failover and failback). •
Windows SMB share = FSx for Windows File Server.
Reference: AWS documentation — https://docs.aws.amazon.com/

stem: A company wants to back up its on-premises intranet application to the AWS Cloud. The company wants to use AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery for the backup solution. The company requires that replication traffic must travel across a private dedicated connection. The application must not be accessible from the public internet. The solution cannot consume more than 75% of the available bandwidth between the on-premises network and AWS. Which combination of steps will meet these requirements? (Select THREE.)

options.text: Create a VPC that has at least two private subnets, two NAT gateways, and a virtual private gateway.
Create a VPC that has at least two public subnets, a virtual private gateway, and an internet gateway.

Create an AWS Site-to-Site VPN connection between the on-premises network and the target AWS network. Configure Quality of Service (QoS) to ensure that the backup does not exceed 75% of the available bandwidth.
Create an AWS Direct Connect connection and a Direct Connect gateway between the on-premises network and the target AWS network.

Configure the replication servers to use private IP addresses for data replication. Configure throttling on the replication instances so that the Elastic Disaster Recovery server bandwidth does not exceed 75% of the available bandwidth.

Configure the recovery instance’s private IP address to match the source server's private IP address. Configure throttling on the recovery instances so that the total bandwidth the recovery instances consume does not exceed 75% of the available bandwidth.

explanation:
D gives the private dedicated path (Direct Connect plus a Direct Connect gateway). A builds the target VPC with private subnets, NAT
gateways for the service endpoints the replication servers need, and a virtual private gateway to attach the private connection. E
makes replication use private IPs and applies the Elastic DR bandwidth throttling setting so replication stays under 75 percent.
wrongOptionsExplanation:
B. Public subnets and an internet gateway contradict the requirement that nothing is exposed to the internet. C. A VPN runs over the
public internet and is not a dedicated connection. QoS is also not how Elastic DR limits bandwidth. F. Matching recovery instance IPs
and throttling recovery instances is wrong: throttling is applied to the replication, not to recovery instances.
plainWords:
Replicate an on-prem app to AWS with Elastic Disaster Recovery over a private dedicated connection, no public exposure, and use no
more than 75 percent of the bandwidth.
keyPoints:
• Elastic DR bandwidth limit = replication throttling setting; private path = Direct Connect plus private IP replication. • Dedicated +
private = Direct Connect, not VPN.
Reference: AWS documentation — https://docs.aws.amazon.com/

stem: A company has an application that runs on Amazon EC2 instances in an Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling group. The company uses AWS CodePipeline to deploy the application. The instances that run in the Auto Scaling group are constantly changing because of scaling events. When the company deploys new application code versions, the company installs the AWS CodeDeploy agent on any new target EC2 instances and associates the instances with the CodeDeploy deployment group. The application is set to go live within the next 24 hours. What should a solutions architect recommend to automate the application deployment process with the LEAST amount of operational overhead?

options.text: Configure Amazon EventBridge to invoke an AWS Lambda function when a new EC2 instance is launched into the Auto Scaling group. Code the Lambda function to associate the EC2 instances with the CodeDeploy deployment group.

Write a script to suspend Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling operations before the deployment of new code When the deployment is complete, create a new AMI and configure the Auto Scaling group's launch template to use the new AMI for new launches. Resume Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling operations.

Create a new AWS CodeBuild project that creates a new AMI that contains the new code Configure CodeBuild to update the Auto Scaling group's launch template to the new AMI. Run an Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling instance refresh operation.

Create a new AMI that has the CodeDeploy agent installed. Configure the Auto Scaling group's launch template to use the new AMI. Associate the CodeDeploy deployment group with the Auto Scaling group instead of the EC2 instances.

explanation:
Bake the CodeDeploy agent into the AMI used by the launch template, and associate the CodeDeploy deployment group with the
Auto Scaling group itself (not with individual instances). New instances launched by scaling are then registered automatically and
receive the latest revision.
wrongOptionsExplanation:
A. A custom Lambda to associate instances is extra code to build and maintain when CodeDeploy already integrates with Auto
Scaling. B. Suspending scaling and manually creating AMIs is risky and manual. C. Building a new AMI on every release with instance
refresh is a valid immutable pattern but a bigger change than needed in 24 hours.
plainWords:
Instances in an Auto Scaling group change constantly. Someone must keep installing the CodeDeploy agent and attaching new
instances to the deployment group. Go live in 24 hours with the least effort.
keyPoints:
• CodeDeploy + Auto Scaling = associate the deployment group with the ASG, agent in the AMI. • Associating with individual
instances breaks when instances are replaced.
Reference: AWS documentation — https://docs.aws.amazon.com/

stem: A company hosts an application on AWS. The application reads and writes objects that are stored in a single Amazon S3 bucket. The company must modify the application to deploy the application in two AWS Regions. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Set up an Amazon CloudFront distribution with the S3 bucket as an origin. Deploy the application to a second Region Modify the application to use the CloudFront distribution. Use AWS Global Accelerator to access the data in the S3 bucket.

Create a new S3 bucket in a second Region. Set up bidirectional S3 Cross-Region Replication (CRR) between the original S3 bucket and the new S3 bucket. Configure an S3 Multi-Region Access Point that uses both S3 buckets. Deploy a modified application to both Regions.

Create a new S3 bucket in a second Region Deploy the application in the second Region. Configure the application to use the new S3 bucket. Set up S3 Cross-Region Replication (CRR) from the original S3 bucket to the new S3 bucket.

Set up an S3 gateway endpoint with the S3 bucket as an origin. Deploy the application to a second Region. Modify the application to use the new S3 gateway endpoint. Use S3 Intelligent-Tiering on the S3 bucket.

explanation:
Create a second bucket in another Region, set up bidirectional Cross-Region Replication, and put an S3 Multi-Region Access Point in
front. The application uses one global endpoint and requests are routed to the closest bucket, and writes in either Region replicate to
the other.
wrongOptionsExplanation:
A. Global Accelerator does not front S3 buckets this way, and CloudFront is mainly a read cache. C. One-way replication means writes
in the second Region never reach the original bucket, so data diverges. D. A gateway endpoint is a regional private path to S3, not a
multi-Region solution.
plainWords: An app uses one S3 bucket. It must now run in two Regions with minimal operational effort.
keyPoints:
• Active-active S3 across Regions = two buckets + two-way CRR + Multi-Region Access Point. • CRR needs versioning on both
buckets.
Reference: AWS documentation — https://docs.aws.amazon.com/

stem: A company is using AWS Organizations with a multi-account architecture. The company's current security configuration for the account architecture includes SCPs, resource-based policies, identity-based policies, trust policies, and session policies. A solutions architect needs to allow an IAM user in Account A to assume a role in Account B. Which combination of steps must the solutions architect take to meet this requirement? (Select THREE.)

options.text: Configure the SCP for Account A to allow the action.
Configure the resource-based policies to allow the action.
Configure the identity-based policy on the user in Account A to allow the action.
Configure the identity-based policy on the user in Account B to allow the action.
Configure the trust policy on the target role in Account B to allow the action.
Configure the session policy to allow the action and to be passed programmatically by the GetSessionToken API operation.

explanation: SOURCE ANSWER B,C,E IS AMBIGUOUS. Required cross-account AssumeRole setup is C (the Account A user has sts:AssumeRole permission) and E (the target role in Account B trusts the user/account). E is itself a resource-based trust policy, so B is redundant if it means an additional resource policy. SCPs in Account A must permit the action, but A is only a configuration change if existing SCPs restrict sts:AssumeRole. D concerns the wrong account's user; F is not how GetSessionToken works. Because the stem says select THREE without clarifying whether SCP changes are needed, do not treat B,C,E as independently confirmed.
wrongOptionsExplanation:
A. An SCP does not grant access. It only needs to avoid blocking it. (See the note below.) D. The user lives in Account A. A policy on a
user in Account B does nothing for this action. F. Session policies only narrow a session after it exists. They are not required to
assume a role.
plainWords: An IAM user in Account A must be able to assume a role in Account B in an organization that uses SCPs and several policy types.
keyPoints:
• Cross-account = permission on the caller side (identity policy) and trust on the target side (role trust policy). • SCPs filter, they
never grant.
HEADS-UP ON THIS QUESTION
• The key says B, C, E. A trust policy is itself the role's resource-based policy, so B and E overlap. In a real design you would also
confirm the SCP in Account A does not deny sts:AssumeRole (option A). If this appears on a test, choose C and E for sure and follow
the wording for the third.
Reference: AWS documentation — https://docs.aws.amazon.com/
SOURCE WARNING: Trust policy and resource-based policy choices overlap.
sourceWarning: Select THREE is ambiguous: trust policy (E) is a resource-based policy (B); SCP permission (A) is conditional on policy configuration.

review.auditNote: AWS docs explicitly call IAM role trust policy a resource-based policy, so B and E are redundant if both are listed. C+E necessary in general, SCP A must not deny but changing SCP depends on its current contents. No unambiguous three-step solution.

wrongOptionsReason.A: SCP must not block AssumeRole; editing is not necessarily needed.
wrongOptionsReason.B: Trust policy E is itself the relevant resource-based policy; redundant wording.

stem: A company plans to consume a third-party software-as-a-service (SaaS) application through APIs. The SaaS provider hosts the application in an AWS VPC, and the company will call it from its own VPC. Security policies require private connectivity without internet traversal, prohibit external access to resources in the company's VPC, and require least-privilege permissions. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Create an AWS PrivateLink interface VPC endpoint. Connect this endpoint to the endpoint service that the third-party SaaS application provides. Create a security group to limit the access to the endpoint. Associate the security group with the endpoint.
Create an AWS Site-to-Site VPN connection between the third-party SaaS provider and the company VPC. Configure network ACLs to limit access across the VPN tunnels.
Create a VPC peering connection between the third-party SaaS provider VPC and the company VPC. Update the route tables with the required peering routes.

Create an AWS PrivateLink endpoint service. Ask the third-party SaaS provider to create an interface VPC endpoint for this endpoint service. Grant permissions for the endpoint service to the specific account of the third-party SaaS provider.

explanation: A is correct. The SaaS provider publishes an AWS PrivateLink endpoint service, and the company creates an interface VPC endpoint as the service consumer. An endpoint security group limits permitted connections; no inbound network path into the company's VPC is exposed to the provider. B is less appropriate: Site-to-Site VPN uses tunnels and adds operational complexity, while the question explicitly asks for AWS-private SaaS access. C uses peering and routing between VPCs, granting broader network-level connectivity than a service-specific endpoint. D reverses the provider and consumer roles: it would let the SaaS provider connect to a service in the company's VPC. Source answer A retained.
wrongOptionsExplanation:
B. A VPN to a SaaS provider is not how SaaS on AWS is consumed and still opens broader network access. C. VPC peering exposes
whole networks both ways and fails with overlapping CIDRs, violating least privilege. D. This reverses the roles: the provider would
connect into your VPC, which violates the rule that your resources cannot be reached from outside.
plainWords:
You must call a SaaS API that runs in its own VPC, privately without the internet, and without exposing anything in your VPC to the
outside, using least privilege.
keyPoints:
• One-way private access to a service = PrivateLink interface endpoint. • The consumer creates the interface endpoint; the provider
creates the endpoint service.
Reference: AWS documentation — https://docs.aws.amazon.com/

stem: A company runs an application on 20 persistent Amazon EC2 instances with multiple attached Amazon EBS volumes. Backups must be stored in a second AWS Region. Recovery of the instances and their configuration must be possible within one business day, with no more than one day's data loss. The company has limited operations staff and already has a CloudFormation template for the network infrastructure in the recovery Region. Which solution best meets the requirements with minimal operational overhead and cost?

options.text: Create another CloudFormation template to recreate the EC2 instances in the secondary Region. Run daily multi-volume snapshots using AWS Systems Manager Automation runbooks, copy the snapshots to the secondary Region, and use the templates and snapshots to recover.

Use Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager (Amazon DLM) to create daily multi-volume EBS snapshots. In a disaster, deploy the CloudFormation template and use DLM to restore the EBS volumes and transfer traffic to the secondary Region.

Use AWS Backup to create a scheduled daily backup plan for the EC2 instances. Configure the backup task to copy the backups to a vault in the secondary Region. In the event of a failure, launch the CloudFormation template, restore the instance volumes and configurations from the backup vault, and transfer usage to the secondary Region.

Deploy equivalent EC2 instances in the secondary Region. Use AWS DataSync daily to copy data from the primary Region. During a disaster, deploy the CloudFormation template and transfer traffic to the secondary Region.

explanation: C is correct. AWS Backup can schedule daily EC2 backups, automatically copy recovery points to a backup vault in another Region, and restore EC2 instances with root and attached EBS data volumes. A could be implemented but requires custom runbook/template orchestration. B is incomplete: DLM manages snapshot lifecycles, not the described EC2 instance recovery and traffic transfer workflow. D requires duplicate running instances and custom data synchronization, increasing cost and effort. Important limitation: AWS Backup does not preserve every instance setting (for example, launch user data); recovery must be tested to establish the one-business-day RTO. Source answer C retained.
wrongOptionsExplanation:
A. Custom Systems Manager runbooks and snapshot copy scripts must be built and maintained. B. Data Lifecycle Manager handles
EBS snapshots only and does not capture the instance configuration or provide the same centralized restore. D. Running a second
fleet and using DataSync is expensive and DataSync does not copy EBS volumes.
plainWords:
20 EC2 instances with many EBS volumes need daily backups copied to another Region, with restore of instances and configuration
inside a day and minimal admin effort.
keyPoints:
• Centralized backup policies, cross-Region and cross-account copy = AWS Backup. • RTO of one day and RPO of one day = backup
and restore strategy.
Reference: AWS documentation — https://docs.aws.amazon.com/

Copy the snapshots to the secondary Region. In the event of a failure, launch the CloudFormation templates, restore the EBS volumes from snapshots, and transfer usage to the secondary Region.

stem: A video-on-demand application serves videos through an Amazon CloudFront distribution with a default cache behavior and one Amazon S3 origin. A second S3 bucket has been configured for Cross-Region Replication (CRR). The company needs CloudFront origin failover to start as quickly as possible, targeting one second after a connection failure, with minimal operational overhead. Which change best meets these requirements?

options.text: Create a second CloudFront distribution that uses the second S3 bucket as a single origin. Create an origin group. Add both distributions to the origin group. Set the original distribution as the primary distribution. Set the new distribution as the secondary distribution. Create an Amazon Route 53 health check to monitor the health of the primary distribution and secondary distribution every second.

Create a new origin in the existing CloudFront distribution. Specify the second S3 bucket as the new origin. Create an origin group. Add the original origin as the primary origin. Add the new origin as the secondary origin. Set the origin response timeout value to 1. Set the origin connection attempts value to 1.

Create a new origin in the existing CloudFront distribution. Specify the second S3 bucket as the new origin. Create an origin group. Add the original origin as the primary origin. Add the new origin as the secondary origin. Update the default cache behavior to use the origin group. Set the origin connection timeout value to 1. Set the origin connection attempts value to 1.

Create a new origin in the existing CloudFront distribution. Specify the second S3 bucket as the new origin. Create an AWS Lambda function to monitor the health of the original origin. Program the Lambda function to update the CloudFront distribution and promote the secondary origin to primary if a health check fails. Create an Amazon EventBridge scheduled rule to invoke the Lambda function every second.

explanation: C is the best offered answer. Add the replicated S3 bucket as a second origin, create an origin group with primary and secondary origins, and configure the default cache behavior to use the group. Set the primary origin connection timeout to 1 second and connection attempts to 1. A incorrectly tries to group separate CloudFront distributions rather than origins. B creates an origin group but does not attach it to the cache behavior; response timeout is not the right lever for standard S3 origins. D introduces unnecessary Lambda automation and EventBridge cannot be scheduled every second. Qualification: the 1-second setting bounds a connection attempt; it does not guarantee all failover scenarios complete within one second. For S3 origins, origin response timeout is not configurable; failover depends on connection errors and configured status codes. Source answer C retained.
wrongOptionsExplanation:
A. Origin groups contain origins, not distributions, and Route 53 health checks cannot achieve sub-second failover. B. It forgets to
point the cache behavior to the origin group, and it changes the response timeout instead of the connection timeout and attempts. D.
A Lambda polling every second to rewrite the distribution is fragile, costly and slower than the built-in origin failover.
plainWords:
CloudFront serves videos from one S3 bucket. A second bucket is replicated with CRR. Failover must start within about 1 second with
the least operational work.
keyPoints:
• CloudFront high availability for origins = origin group with primary and secondary, and the behavior must use it. • Fast failover
tuning = connection timeout and connection attempts.
Reference: AWS documentation — https://docs.aws.amazon.com/

stem: A company is running an application in the AWS Cloud. The application uses AWS Lambda functions and Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) containers that run with AWS Fargate technology as its primary compute. The load on the application is irregular. The application experiences long periods of no usage, followed by sudden and significant increases and decreases in traffic. The application is write-heavy and stores data in an Amazon Aurora MySQL database. The database runs on an Amazon RDS memory optimized DB instance that is not able to handle the load. What is the MOST cost-effective way for the company to handle the sudden and significant changes in traffic?

options.text: Add additional read replicas to the database. Purchase Instance Savings Plans and RDS Reserved Instances.
Migrate the database to an Aurora multi-master DB cluster. Purchase Instance Savings Plans.
Migrate the database to an Aurora global database. Purchase Compute Savings Plans and RDS Reserved Instances.
Migrate the database to Aurora Serverless v2. Purchase Compute Savings Plans.

explanation: Corrected study wording (original option D specified retired Aurora Serverless v1): Aurora Serverless v2 automatically adjusts database capacity for unpredictable and write-heavy workloads, avoiding continuously provisioned peak capacity. Compute Savings Plans apply to Lambda and Fargate compute. A adds readers rather than scaling writes; B uses a legacy multi-master design; C adds global replication rather than elastic writer capacity. Original question and option are retained in originalQuestionSnapshot.
wrongOptionsExplanation:
A. Read replicas help reads, not a write-heavy load, and Instance Savings Plans plus reserved instances commit you to capacity you
often do not use. B. Multi-master clusters are not designed for unpredictable scaling and commitments do not fit an irregular load. C.
Aurora Global Database is for cross-Region DR and low-latency reads, not for absorbing bursts.
plainWords:
Usage is idle for long periods, then spikes suddenly. The write-heavy Aurora MySQL instance cannot cope. Find the most
cost-effective way to handle the swings.
keyPoints:
• Unpredictable or intermittent database load = Aurora Serverless. • Commitments (RI/Savings Plans) suit steady usage, not spiky
usage.
HEADS-UP ON THIS QUESTION
• Aurora Serverless v1 has been retired or scheduled for retirement. Today the modern answer for this pattern is Aurora Serverless v2
(which can also scale down to very low capacity). The reasoning is the same.
Reference: AWS documentation — https://docs.aws.amazon.com/
SOURCE WARNING: Aurora Serverless v1 is obsolete; consult current Aurora Serverless v2 guidance.

stem: A company runs a data-intensive monthly reporting job on hundreds of EC2 instances. Its shared file system, hosted on always-on EC2 instances, contains 200 TB of data. Each 72-hour job reads and modifies only a subset of files. Compute scales down between jobs, but the file servers remain running. Which replacement for the shared storage offers the greatest likely cost reduction while maintaining high-performance file access during each run?

options.text: Migrate the data from the existing shared file system to an Amazon S3 bucket that uses the S3 Intelligent-Tiering storage class. Before the job runs each month, use Amazon FSx for Lustre to create a new file system with the data from Amazon S3 by using lazy loading. Use the new file system as the shared storage for the duration of the job. Delete the file system when the job is complete.

Migrate the data from the existing shared file system to a large Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) volume with Multi-Attach enabled. Attach the EBS volume to each of the instances by using a user data script in the Auto Scaling group launch template. Use the EBS volume as the shared storage for the duration of the job. Detach the EBS volume when the job is complete.

Migrate the data from the existing shared file system to an Amazon S3 bucket that uses the S3 Standard storage class. Before the job runs each month, use Amazon FSx for Lustre to create a new file system with the data from Amazon S3 by using batch loading. Use the new file system as the shared storage for the duration of the job. Delete the file system when the job is complete.

Migrate the data from the existing shared file system to an Amazon S3 bucket. Before the job runs each month, use AWS Storage Gateway to create a file gateway with the data from Amazon S3. Use the file gateway as the shared storage for the job. Delete the file gateway when the job is complete.

explanation: A is the best choice among the supplied options. Store the durable dataset in S3 Intelligent-Tiering and create an FSx for Lustre file system for each monthly run, linked to S3. File metadata is imported and file contents are loaded on first access, so unaccessed content need not be fully copied. Export modified files back to S3 before deleting the temporary file system; this persistence step is essential and is omitted from the source option. B fails because EBS Multi-Attach is limited in attachment count and needs a cluster-aware file system. C uses full batch loading and S3 Standard, potentially transferring more than the subset used. D uses File Gateway, not a comparable high-performance parallel file system. Exact cost ranking depends on access pattern and S3 tiering fees; the source's absolute 'largest' claim is not provable without measurements.
wrongOptionsExplanation:
B. EBS Multi-Attach supports only a limited number of instances in a single AZ, far fewer than hundreds, and is not a shared file
system. C. Batch loading all 200 TB into Lustre wastes time and money when only a subset of files is needed. D. A File Gateway is for
hybrid access and does not provide the high-performance parallel throughput the job needs.
plainWords:
200 TB on always-on EC2 file servers, used only for a 72-hour monthly job that reads a subset of files. Replace it to cut cost while
keeping high performance during the job.
keyPoints:
• Temporary HPC file system on S3 data = FSx for Lustre (scratch) linked to S3. • Lazy loading fetches only the files you read.
Reference: AWS documentation — https://docs.aws.amazon.com/

stem: An events company operates a ticketing platform on Amazon ECS backed by EC2 On-Demand instances in an Auto Scaling group. Customer event dates and times are known in advance, and the Auto Scaling group currently uses predictive scaling. ECS tasks frequently download ticket assets from an S3 bucket in the same Region and account, but this traffic currently passes through a NAT gateway. Which TWO changes reduce costs without compromising availability?

options.text: Create a gateway VPC endpoint for the S3 bucket
Add another ECS capacity provider that uses an Auto Scaling group of Spot Instances Configure the new capacity provider strategy to have the same weight as the existing capacity provider strategy
Create On-Demand Capacity Reservations for the applicable instance type for the time period of the scheduled scaling policies
Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration on the S3 bucket
Replace the predictive scaling policy with scheduled scaling policies for the scheduled events

explanation: A removes NAT gateway data-processing costs for S3 traffic by using an S3 gateway VPC endpoint, provided route tables and policies are configured. B adds a Spot-backed ECS capacity provider alongside existing On-Demand capacity, reducing average compute costs; availability depends on keeping sufficient On-Demand baseline capacity and making workloads resilient to Spot interruptions. C reserves On-Demand capacity but is not itself a discount. D S3 Transfer Acceleration is not useful for same-Region private traffic. E scheduled scaling may be useful for known events, but replacing predictive scaling is not inherently a cost reduction and risks missing unexpected load. Source A+B retained with Spot-availability caveat.
wrongOptionsExplanation:
C. Capacity Reservations add commitment cost rather than reduce it. D. Transfer Acceleration is for long-distance uploads and adds
cost. The cluster and bucket are in the same Region. E. Replacing predictive scaling with scheduled scaling does not make compute
cheaper and may reduce flexibility.
plainWords: An ECS cluster on On-Demand EC2 downloads lots of S3 assets through a NAT gateway. Cut cost without lowering availability.
keyPoints:
• NAT gateway charges for S3 or DynamoDB traffic = use a gateway endpoint. • Mix On-Demand and Spot with ECS capacity
providers to cut cost safely.
Reference: AWS documentation — https://docs.aws.amazon.com/

stem: A company hosts an API with a Regional Amazon API Gateway endpoint and AWS Lambda in one Region. The API calls a vendor service using a credential stored in Secrets Manager and encrypted with a customer-managed KMS key, and reads and writes a DynamoDB global table. The company needs active-active API deployment across multiple AWS Regions with minimal operational overhead. Which THREE changes best meet these requirements?

options.text: Deploy the API to multiple Regions. Configure Amazon Route 53 with custom domain names that route traffic to each Regional API endpoint. Implement a Route 53 multivalue answer routing policy.
Create a new KMS multi-Region customer managed key. Create a new KMS customer managed replica key in each in-scope Region.
Replicate the existing Secrets Manager secret to other Regions. For each in-scope Region's replicated secret, select the appropriate KMS key.
Create a new AWS managed KMS key in each in-scope Region. Convert an existing key to a multi-Region key. Use the multi-Region key in other Regions.
Create a new Secrets Manager secret in each in-scope Region. Copy the secret value from the existing Region to the new secret in each in-scope Region.

Modify the deployment process for the Lambda function to repeat the deployment across in-scope Regions. Turn on the multi-Region option for the existing API. Select the Lambda function that is deployed in each Region as the backend for the multi-Region API.

explanation: A+B+C are the intended choices. A deploys regional API endpoints and uses Route 53 DNS routing; multivalue routing distributes healthy endpoint answers but is not a strict global load balancer. B creates a multi-Region customer-managed KMS key and regional replicas. C replicates the existing secret to other Regions with the selected regional KMS keys, so credential updates can propagate. D cannot convert an existing single-Region key to multi-Region and AWS-managed keys are not created that way. E creates manually managed secrets that can drift. F incorrectly asserts a native 'multi-Region option' on an existing API Gateway API. Note: option A alone does not explicitly state deploying the Lambda functions in each Region; regional Lambda deployments are an additional implementation requirement.
wrongOptionsExplanation:
D. AWS managed keys cannot be converted to multi-Region keys. E. Manually copying secrets to each Region creates operational
overhead and drift. F. API Gateway does not have a "multi-Region option" to attach per-Region Lambda backends like that. You
deploy the API per Region.
plainWords:
An API Gateway + Lambda + DynamoDB global table API must become active-active in several Regions. Its vendor API key is in
Secrets Manager encrypted with a customer managed KMS key.
keyPoints:
• Multi-Region encryption = KMS multi-Region keys; multi-Region secrets = Secrets Manager replication. • Active-active API = deploy
in each Region and route with Route 53.
Reference: AWS documentation — https://docs.aws.amazon.com/

The company wants a hub-and-spoke architecture that routes all private-subnet internet traffic through an existing NAT gateway in a centralized egress VPC. Which additional steps meet this requirement?

options.text: Create peering connections between the egress VPC and the spoke VPCs. Configure the required routing to allow access to the internet.
Create a transit gateway, and share it with the existing AWS accounts. Attach existing VPCs to the transit gateway Configure the required routing to allow access to the internet.
Create a transit gateway in every account. Attach the NAT gateway to the transit gateways. Configure the required routing to allow access to the internet.
Create an AWS PrivateLink connection between the egress VPC and the spoke VPCs. Configure the required routing to allow access to the internet

explanation: B is correct. Create and share an AWS Transit Gateway across accounts (for example using AWS RAM), attach the spoke and egress VPCs, and configure VPC and transit-gateway route tables so spoke default routes reach the egress VPC and return traffic reaches the correct spoke. A VPC peering does not provide transitive routing through a peer's internet gateway/NAT gateway. C proposes a transit gateway per account and incorrectly attaches a NAT gateway directly to transit gateways. D PrivateLink exposes specific endpoint services, not general internet egress. Centralized egress adds Transit Gateway processing charges and must be designed for high availability across AZs.
wrongOptionsExplanation:
A. Peering is non-transitive and cannot use another VPC's NAT gateway. It also does not scale to hundreds of VPCs. C. You do not
create a Transit Gateway in every account, and you cannot attach a NAT gateway to one. D. PrivateLink exposes specific services, it is
not a general internet egress path.
plainWords: Hundreds of accounts need their private subnets to reach the internet through one NAT gateway in a central egress VPC.
keyPoints:
• Hub-and-spoke, many accounts, central egress = Transit Gateway + RAM + egress VPC. • VPC peering is not transitive.
Reference: AWS documentation — https://docs.aws.amazon.com/

stem: A company is migrating an on-premises web application to EC2 instances in private subnets behind a public Application Load Balancer. The application calls a third-party API whose firewall permits only one customer-owned public CIDR block. Internet-bound requests from the private instances use NAT gateways. How can the company preserve API access after migration?

options.text: Associate a block of customer-owned public IP addresses to the VPC. Enable public IP addressing for public subnets in the VPC.
Register a block of customer-owned public IP addresses in the AWS account. Create Elastic IP addresses from the address block and assign them lo the NAT gateways in the VPC.
Create Elastic IP addresses from the block of customer-owned IP addresses. Assign the static Elastic IP addresses to the ALB.
Register a block of customer-owned public IP addresses in the AWS account. Set up AWS Global Accelerator to use Elastic IP addresses from the address block. Set the ALB as the accelerator endpoint.

explanation: B is correct. Register the customer-owned public IPv4 prefix using Bring Your Own IP (BYOIP), allocate Elastic IP addresses from it, and associate them with the public NAT gateways. The third party sees the NAT gateways' public egress IP addresses; ensure all such addresses fall within the permitted CIDR. A merely assigns public addressing to public subnets and does not control private-instance NAT egress. C is invalid because ALBs do not accept static Elastic IP associations and are inbound-facing here. D uses Global Accelerator for inbound application traffic, not outbound API requests from private EC2 instances. The question assumes the customer owns the allowed prefix.
wrongOptionsExplanation:
A. Associating a block to a VPC and enabling public IPs on subnets does not control the NAT source address. C. ALBs cannot be
assigned Elastic IPs, and inbound ALB addresses are not the outbound source addresses. D. Global Accelerator provides static
inbound IPs for users, not the outbound source address for calls to a vendor.
plainWords:
A third party allows only one public CIDR block. The app will run behind an ALB with instances in private subnets that use NAT
gateways for outbound calls.
keyPoints:
• Source IP of outbound calls from private subnets = NAT gateway Elastic IP. • Need your existing IP range in AWS = BYOIP.
Reference: AWS documentation — https://docs.aws.amazon.com/

stem: A gaming company is rehosting a compute-intensive application on AWS. It runs a Node.js application on Ubuntu EC2 compute-optimized instances and currently uses an on-premises Redis instance to maintain frequently updated leaderboards. Which architecture best preserves performance after migration?

options.text: Create an Auto Scaling group of memory optimized Amazon EC2 Spot Instances behind an Application Load Balancer. Use an Amazon ElastiCache (Redis OSS) cluster to maintain the leaderboard.
Create an Auto Scaling group of compute optimized Amazon EC2 Spot Instances behind an Application Load Balancer. Use an Amazon OpenSearch Service cluster to maintain the leaderboard.
Create an Auto Scaling group of compute optimized Amazon EC2 On-Demand Instances behind an Application Load Balancer. Use an Amazon ElastiCache (Redis OSS) cluster to maintain the leaderboard.
Create an Auto Scaling group of memory optimized Amazon EC2 On-Demand Instances behind an Application Load Balancer. Use an Amazon DynamoDB table to maintain the leaderboard.

explanation: C is the best choice. Compute-optimized On-Demand EC2 instances support CPU-intensive application work with no Spot interruption risk, while ElastiCache for Redis OSS supports frequently updated leaderboards using sorted sets. A switches to memory-optimized Spot instances, mismatching compute requirements and introducing interruption risk. B uses OpenSearch for a workload already modeled in Redis and adds Spot interruption risk. D also changes the compute profile and replaces Redis with DynamoDB, requiring a leaderboard data-model change. Redis sorted sets support efficient score and ranking updates.
wrongOptionsExplanation:
A. Memory optimized Spot instances are the wrong shape for compute-heavy HPC and Spot interruptions hurt live games. B.
OpenSearch is a search and analytics engine, not a leaderboard store. D. Memory optimized instances do not match the compute
need and moving to DynamoDB requires redesigning the Redis logic.
plainWords: A game rehosted on EC2 needs HPC-class compute and a fast leaderboard that currently runs on an on-prem Redis instance.
keyPoints:
• Leaderboard / sorted sets / existing Redis = ElastiCache for Redis. • Compute-heavy = compute optimized (C family).
Reference: AWS documentation — https://docs.aws.amazon.com/

Create an Auto Scaling group of compute optimized Amazon EC2 Spot Instances behind an Application Load Balancer. Use an Amazon OpenSearch Service cluster to maintain the leaderboard.

stem: An e-commerce company needs a simple, highly available, loosely coupled order-processing application. Order traffic is sporadic, with spikes during marketing campaigns. Orders must be processed promptly and stored in DynamoDB. Which architecture is the most reliable?

options.text: Receive the orders in an Amazon EC2-hosted database and use EC2 instances to process them.
Receive the orders in an Amazon SQS queue and invoke an AWS Lambda function to processthem.
Receive the orders using the AWS Step Functions program and launch an Amazon ECS container to process them.
Receive the orders in Amazon Kinesis Data Streams and use Amazon EC2 instances to process them.

explanation: B is correct. SQS durably buffers incoming orders, and an SQS-triggered Lambda function scales processing before writing to DynamoDB. Configure a dead-letter queue, appropriate visibility timeout, retries, and idempotent writes because SQS and Lambda processing can be at least once. A couples intake and processing to EC2-hosted components. C uses Step Functions and ECS but adds orchestration complexity for straightforward asynchronous queue processing. D uses Kinesis and EC2, requiring shard/consumer capacity management without a demonstrated streaming requirement.
wrongOptionsExplanation:
A. A database on EC2 plus EC2 processors is tightly coupled and needs scaling and patching. C. Step Functions as the intake point
with ECS tasks is more complex than needed for simple order queuing. D. Kinesis with EC2 consumers requires shard management
and server operations for a sporadic workload.
plainWords: A simple, highly available, loosely coupled order pipeline with sporadic traffic and spikes during campaigns.
keyPoints:
• Decouple + buffer + auto scale + minimal ops = SQS + Lambda. • Add a dead-letter queue for failed messages.
Reference: AWS documentation — https://docs.aws.amazon.com/

The application is responsible for receiving and processing orders before storing them in an Amazon DynamoDB table. The application has a sporadic traffic pattern and should be able to scale during marketing campaigns to process the orders with minimal delays. Receive the orders in an Amazon SQS queue and invoke an AWS Lambda function to processthem.

stem: A company runs EC2 applications in private VPC subnets that use NAT gateways across multiple Availability Zones for internet access. It must identify outbound internet destinations and block access to selected websites. VPC Flow Logs already capture traffic on the NAT gateways' network interfaces. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Use Amazon CloudWatch Logs Insights to query the logs and determine the internet destinations that the EC2 instances communicate with. Use AWS Network Firewall to blockthe websites.
Use Amazon CloudWatch Logs Insights to query the logs and determine the internet destinations that the EC2 instances communicate with. Use AWS WAF to block the websites.

Use the BytesInFromSource and BytesInFromDestination Amazon CloudWatch metrics to determine the internet destinations that the EC2 instances communicate with. Use AWS Network Firewall to block the websites.
Use the BytesInFromSource and BytesInFromDestination Amazon CloudWatch metrics to determine the internet destinations that the EC2 instances communicate with. Use AWS WAF to block the websites.

explanation: A is the best offered answer. CloudWatch Logs Insights can analyze NAT interface VPC Flow Logs to identify destination IP addresses, while AWS Network Firewall can filter outbound traffic using domain-based or stateful rules when routed through firewall endpoints. Important caveat: VPC Flow Logs do not record domain names or URLs; add Network Firewall logs, DNS logs, or other application-layer telemetry to identify websites by name. B and D incorrectly use AWS WAF, which protects HTTP(S) applications and is not a general outbound NAT egress filter. C and D rely on CloudWatch byte-count metrics that cannot identify destinations. Firewall routing and AZ-aware deployment are required.
wrongOptionsExplanation:
B. AWS WAF protects HTTP traffic to CloudFront, ALB or API Gateway. It does not filter outbound traffic from a NAT gateway. C.
CloudWatch NAT metrics show byte totals, not the destinations. D. Same metrics problem, and WAF is the wrong place to block
egress.
plainWords:
You need to identify which internet destinations EC2 instances contact through NAT gateways and block specific sites. VPC Flow Logs
already exist.
keyPoints:
• Outbound domain filtering = Network Firewall (or DNS Firewall for DNS lookups). • WAF = inbound web requests. Flow Logs = who
talked to whom.
Reference: AWS documentation — https://docs.aws.amazon.com/

Use Amazon CloudWatch Logs Insights to query the logs and determine the internet destinations that the EC2 instances communicate with. Use AWS WAF to block the websites.
