stem: A company needs to audit the security posture of a newly acquired AWS account. The company’s data security team requires a notification only when an Amazon S3 bucket becomes publicly exposed. The company has already established an Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) topic that has the data security team's email address subscribed. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Create an S3 event notification on all S3 buckets for the isPublic event. Select the SNS topic as the target for the event notifications.

Create an analyzer in AWS Identity and Access Management Access Analyzer. Create an Amazon EventBridge rule for the event type “Access Analyzer Finding” with a filter for “isPublic: true.” Select the SNS topic as the EventBridge rule target.
Create an Amazon EventBridge rule for the event type “Bucket-Level API Call via CloudTrail” with a filter for “PutBucketPolicy.” Select the SNS topic as the EventBridge rule target.

Activate AWS Config and add the cloudtrail-s3-dataevents-enabled rule. Create an Amazon EventBridge rule for the event type “Config Rules Re-evaluation Status” with a filter for “NON_COMPLIANT.” Select the SNS topic as the EventBridge rule target.

explanation:
IAM Access Analyzer (external access analyzer) generates findings when a bucket is accessible publicly or from outside the account.
An EventBridge rule filtered on the finding with isPublic = true sends only those events to the SNS topic.
wrongOptionsExplanation:
A. S3 event notifications have no isPublic event type. C. A PutBucketPolicy rule fires on every bucket policy change, not just those
that make a bucket public. D. The Config rule named does not detect public buckets (it checks that CloudTrail data events are
enabled).
plainWords: Notify the security team only when an S3 bucket becomes publicly exposed.
keyPoints:
• Detect resources shared publicly or externally = IAM Access Analyzer (EventBridge + SNS to alert). • Block Public Access is the
preventive control.
Reference: AWS documentation — https://docs.aws.amazon.com/

stem: A software company needs to create short-lived test environments to test pull requests as part of its development process. Each test environment consists of a single Amazon EC2 instance that is in an Auto Scaling group. The test environments must be able to communicate with a central server to report test results. The central server is located in an on-premises data center. A solutions architect must implement a solution so that the company can create and delete test environments without any manual intervention. The company has created a transit gateway with a VPN attachment to the on-premises network. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Create an AWS CloudFormation template that contains a transit gateway attachment and related routing configurations. Create a CloudFormation stack set that includes this template. Use CloudFormation StackSets to deploy a new stack for each VPC in the account. Deploy a new VPC for each test environment.
Create a single VPC for the test environments. Include a transit gateway attachment and related routing configurations. Use AWS CloudFormation to deploy all test environments into the VPC.

Create a new OU in AWS Organizations for testing. Create an AWS CloudFormation template that contains a VPC, necessary networking resources, a transit gateway attachment, and related routing configurations. Create a CloudFormation stack set that includes this template. Use CloudFormation StackSets for deployments into each account under the testing 01.1. Create a new account for each test environment.

Convert the test environment EC2 instances into Docker images. Use AWS CloudFormation to configure an Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) cluster in a new VPC, create a transit gateway attachment, and create related routing configurations. Use Kubernetes to manage the deployment and lifecycle of the test environments.

explanation:
Create one VPC for test environments with the transit gateway attachment and routes set up once. CloudFormation then deploys
each test environment (EC2 and Auto Scaling group) into that shared VPC and deletes it on demand. The connectivity never changes,
so there is no repeated network setup.
wrongOptionsExplanation:
A. A new VPC and transit gateway attachment for every test run is a lot of repeated provisioning. C. Creating a new account per test
environment is far heavier than needed. D. Containerizing everything and running EKS is a large redesign.
plainWords:
Each pull request gets a test environment that must reach an on-prem server through an existing transit gateway and VPN. Automate
create and delete with minimal effort.
keyPoints:
• Build the network once, deploy workloads many times on top of it.
Reference: AWS documentation — https://docs.aws.amazon.com/

stem: A company is migrating a monolithic on-premises .NET Framework production application to AWS. Application demand will grow exponentially in the next 6 months. The company must ensure that the application can scale appropriately. The application currently connects to a Microsoft SQL Server transactional database. The company has well-documented source code for the application. Some business logic is contained within stored procedures. A solutions architect must recommend a solution to redesign the application to meet the growth in demand. Which solution will meet this requirement MOST cost-effectively?

options.text: Use Amazon API Gateway APIs and Amazon EC2 Spot Instances to rehost the application with a scalable microservices architecture. Deploy the EC2 instances in a cluster placement group. Configure EC2 Auto Scaling. Store the data and stored procedures in Amazon RDS for SQL Server.

Use AWS Application Migration Service to migrate the application to AWS Elastic Beanstalk. Deploy Elastic Beanstalk packages to configure and deploy the application as microservices. Deploy Elastic Beanstalk across multiple Availability Zones and configure auto scaling. Store the data and stored procedures in Amazon RDS for MySQL.

Migrate the applications by using AWS App2Container. Use AWS Fargate in multiple AWS Regions to host the containers. Use Amazon API Gateway APIs and AWS Lambda functions to call the containers. Store the data and stored procedures in Amazon DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX).

Use Amazon API Gateway APIs and AWS Lambda functions to decouple the application into microservices. Use the AWS Schema Conversion Tool (AWS SCT) to review and modify the stored procedures. Store the data in Amazon Aurora Serverless v2.

explanation: Verified answer D (this JSON option order). API Gateway and Lambda allow the documented monolith to be refactored into independently scaling microservices; AWS SCT assesses and converts supported SQL Server schemas and stored procedures for an Aurora-compatible relational database; Aurora Serverless v2 adjusts capacity automatically. Important: existing .NET Framework binaries cannot simply run unchanged in a managed Lambda .NET runtime; port/rewrite to supported modern .NET and remediate incompatible dependencies. Stored procedure conversion can require manual work and testing. Cost-effectiveness is the intended architectural comparison, not a guarantee of lowest cost at all utilization levels.
wrongOptionsExplanation: A: Spot interruptions and cluster placement groups are poor choices for a production web-service redesign, while retaining SQL Server licensing costs; no convincing microservice decomposition plan. B: AWS Application Migration Service is a rehosting tool, not a monolith-to-Elastic-Beanstalk microservice conversion mechanism; SQL Server procedures need conversion before MySQL. C: Fargate containers may be useful, but multi-Region adds cost/complexity, and DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) is a DynamoDB cache that cannot store/execute relational stored procedures. D: Correct intended serverless modernization solution, with application porting and database code conversion required.
plainWords: A legacy .NET Framework monolith and SQL Server stored procedures must be redesigned to handle rapid growth without excessive infrastructure cost.
keyPoints: Correct D. API Gateway + Lambda for scalable microservices; AWS SCT for SQL Server schema and stored-procedure assessment/conversion; Aurora Serverless v2 for variable relational database demand. Must port legacy .NET Framework code to modern .NET for Lambda. External exact-match questions: https://www.freecram.net/question/Amazon.SAP-C02.v2025-04-03.q227/a-company-is-migrating-a-monolithic-on-premises-.net-framework-production-application-to-aws-application ; https://www.certstopics.com/questions/amazon-web-services-sap-c02-actual-questions.html ; AWS: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/lambda-csharp.html ; https://docs.aws.amazon.com/pdfs/dms/latest/sql-server-to-aurora-postgresql-migration-playbook/dms-mpb-sql-server-to-aurora-postgresql.pdf
sourceWarning: External copies confirm the serverless option but reorder choices: Freecram labels it C, while this bank and Certstopics label it D. Original stem and option text preserved. Legacy .NET Framework must be modernized; SCT may not automatically convert all stored procedures.

stem: A company has a complex web application that leverages Amazon CloudFront for global scalability and performance Over time, users report that the web application is slowing down The company's operations team reports that the CloudFront cache hit ratio has been dropping steadily. The cache metrics report indicates that query strings on some URLs are inconsistently ordered and are specified sometimes in mixed-case letters and sometimes in lowercase letters. Which set of actions should the solutions architect take to increase the cache hit ratio as quickly as possible?

options.text: Deploy a Lambda@Edge function to sort parameters by name and force them lo be lowercase Select the CloudFront viewer request trigger to invoke the function
Update the CloudFront distribution to disable caching based on query string parameters.
Deploy a reverse proxy after the load balancer to post-process the emitted URLs in the application to force the URL strings to be lowercase.
Update the CloudFront distribution to specify casing-insensitive query string processing.

explanation:
Normalize the URLs at the edge. A Lambda@Edge function on the viewer request event can sort the query string parameters and
lowercase them, so equivalent requests produce the same cache key.
wrongOptionsExplanation:
B. Ignoring query strings entirely would serve the wrong content when parameters change the response. C. A reverse proxy behind
the load balancer is after the cache, so it does not improve the cache hit ratio, and it adds infrastructure. D. CloudFront has no
"case-insensitive query string" setting.
plainWords:
The CloudFront cache hit ratio is falling because the same URLs arrive with query strings in different orders and letter cases, so each
looks like a different object.
keyPoints:
• Poor cache hit ratio from inconsistent URLs = normalize the cache key (Lambda@Edge or CloudFront Functions at viewer request).
HEADS-UP ON THIS QUESTION
• Today a CloudFront Function can do this cheaper and faster than Lambda@Edge. The idea is the same.
Reference: AWS documentation — https://docs.aws.amazon.com/

stem: A financial services company in North America plans to release a new online web application to its customers on AWS . The company will launch the application in the us- east-1 Region on Amazon EC2 instances. The application must be highly available and must dynamically scale to meet user traffic. The company also wants to implement a disaster recovery environment for the application in the us-west-1 Region by using active- passive failover. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Create a VPC in us-east-1 and a VPC in us-west-1 Configure VPC peering In the us- east-1VPC. create an Application Load Balancer (ALB) that extends across multiple Availability Zones in both VPCs Create an Auto Scaling group that deploys the EC2 instances across the multiple Availability Zones in both VPCs Place the Auto Scaling group behind the ALB.

Create a VPC in us-east-1 and a VPC in us-west-1. In the us-east-1 VPC. create an Application Load Balancer (ALB) that extends across multiple Availability Zones in that VPC. Create an Auto Scaling group that deploys the EC2 instances across the multiple Availability Zones in the us-east-1 VPC Place the Auto Scaling group behind the ALB Set up the same configuration in the us-west-1 VPC. Create an Amazon Route 53 hosted zone Create separate records for each ALB Enable health checks to ensure high availability between Regions.

Create a VPC in us-east-1 and a VPC in us-west-1 In the us-east-1 VPC. create an Application Load Balancer (ALB) that extends across multiple Availability Zones in that VPC Create an Auto Scaling group that deploys the EC2 instances across the multiple Availability Zones in the us-east-1 VPC Place the Auto Scaling group behind the ALB Set up the same configuration in the us-west-1 VPC Create an Amazon Route 53 hosted zone. Create separate records for each ALB Enable health checks and configure a failover routing policy for each record.

Create a VPC in us-east-1 and a VPC in us-west-1 Configure VPC peering In the us- east-1 VPC. create an Application Load Balancer (ALB) that extends across multiple Availability Zones in Create an Auto Scaling group that deploys the EC2 instances across the multiple Availability Zones in both VPCs Place the Auto Scaling group behind the ALB Create an Amazon Route 53 host.. Create a record for the ALB.

explanation:
Build the same stack (ALB, Auto Scaling group across AZs) in each Region. Create Route 53 records for each ALB with health checks,
and configure a failover routing policy with us-east-1 as primary and us-west-1 as secondary.
wrongOptionsExplanation:
A. An ALB and Auto Scaling group cannot span two Regions, even with peering. B. Separate records with health checks but no failover
policy do not give active-passive behavior. D. Same impossible cross-Region ALB and no health-based failover.
plainWords: A web app in us-east-1 needs high availability and a passive DR environment in us-west-1.
keyPoints:
• Load balancers and Auto Scaling groups are Regional. Cross-Region failover = Route 53 failover routing + health checks.
Reference: AWS documentation — https://docs.aws.amazon.com/

stem: A company has 10 accounts that are part of an organization in AWS Organizations AWS Config is configured in each account All accounts belong to either the Prod OU or the NonProd OU The company has set up an Amazon EventBridge rule in each AWS account to notify an Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) topic when an Amazon EC2 security group inbound rule is created with 0.0.0.0/0 as the source The company's security team is subscribed to the SNS topic For all accounts in the NonProd OU the security team needs to remove the ability to create a security group inbound rule that includes 0.0.0.0/0 as the source Which solution will meet this requirement with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Modify the EventBridge rule to invoke an AWS Lambda function to remove the security group inbound rule and to publish to the SNS topic Deploy the updated rule to the NonProd OU
Add the vpc-sg-open-only-to-authorized-ports AWS Config managed rule to the NonProd OU
Configure an SCP to allow the ec2 AulhonzeSecurityGrouplngress action when the value of the aws Sourcelp condition key is not 0.0.0.0/0 Apply the SCP to the NonProd OU
Configure an SCP to deny the ec2 AuthorizeSecurityGrouplngress action when the value of the aws Sourcelp condition key is 0.0.0.0/0 Apply the SCP to the NonProd OU

explanation:
An SCP applied to the NonProd OU is a preventive control that applies to all current and future accounts in the OU. A deny on
ec2:AuthorizeSecurityGroupIngress with a condition on the open CIDR blocks the action before it happens.
wrongOptionsExplanation:
A. A Lambda that removes rules after the fact is reactive and you must build and deploy it. B. A Config managed rule only detects
noncompliance and does not stop it. C. Using an allow with a negated condition does not work well with SCP semantics and still does
not deny by default.
plainWords:
In NonProd accounts, nobody should be able to create a security group rule that opens inbound access to 0.0.0.0/0, with the least
overhead.
keyPoints:
• Prevent (not just detect) org-wide = SCP. Detect = Config.
HEADS-UP ON THIS QUESTION
• In real life, aws:SourceIp is the caller's IP address, not the CIDR inside the rule, so an SCP cannot reliably inspect the rule contents.
The exam answer is the SCP deny. In practice use Config auto-remediation or Firewall Manager security group policies.
Reference: AWS documentation — https://docs.aws.amazon.com/

stem: A company has an online learning platform that teaches data science. The platform uses the AWS Cloud to provision on-demand lab environments for its students. Each student receives a dedicated AWS account for a short time. Students need access to ml.p2.xlarge instances to run a single Amazon SageMaker machine learning training job and to deploy the inference endpoint. Account provisioning is automated. The accounts are members of an organization in AWS Organizations with all features enabled. The accounts must be provisioned in the ap-southeast-2 Region. The default resource usage quotas are not sufficient for the accounts. A solutions architect must enhance the account provisioning process to include automated quota increases. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Create a quota request template in the us-east-1 Region in the organization's management account. Enable template association. Add a quota for SageMaker in ap- southeast-2 for ml.p2.xlarge training job usage. Set the desired quota to 1. Add a quota for SageMaker in ap-southeast-2 for ml.p2.xlarge endpoint usage. Set the desired quota to 1.

Create a quota request template in the us-east-1 Region in the organization's management account. Enable template association. Add a quota for SageMaker in ap- southeast-2 for ml.p2.xlarge training warm pool usage. Set the desired quota to 2.

Create a quota request template in ap-southeast-2 in the organization's management account. Enable template association. Add a quota for SageMaker in the us-east-1 Region for ml.p2.xlarge training job usage. Set the desired quota to 1. Add a quota for SageMaker in us-east-1 for ml.p2.xlarge endpoint usage. Set the desired quota to 1.

Create a quota request template in ap-southeast-2 in the organization's management account. Enable template association. Add a quota for SageMaker in the us-east-1 Region for ml.p2.xlarge training warm pool usage. Set the desired quota to 2.

explanation:
Service Quotas request templates live in the management account in us-east-1. You add the target quota (in ap-southeast-2) for both
training jobs and endpoints, set the desired value to 1 each, and enable template association so every new organization account
automatically gets the requests.
wrongOptionsExplanation:
B. Warm pool usage is a different quota, and 2 is not what the students need. C. The template is not created in ap-southeast-2, and
the quotas are requested for us-east-1 instead of the required Region. D. Both the template Region and the target Region are wrong.
plainWords: Student accounts need SageMaker ml.p2.xlarge quotas increased automatically in ap-southeast-2 when each account is created.
keyPoints:
• Org-wide automatic quota increases = Service Quotas request template in us-east-1 with association enabled.
Reference: AWS documentation — https://docs.aws.amazon.com/

stem: A company runs an application on Amazon EC2 and AWS Lambda. The application stores temporary data in Amazon S3. The S3 objects are deleted after 24 hours. The company deploys new versions of the application by launching AWS CloudFormation stacks. The stacks create the required resources. After validating a new version, the company deletes the old stack. The deletion of an old development stack recently failed. A solutions architect needs to resolve this issue without major architecture changes. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Create a Lambda function to delete objects from the S3 bucket. Add the Lambda function as a custom resource in the CloudFormation stack with a DependsOn attribute that points to the S3 bucket resource.
Modify the CloudFormation stack to attach a DeletionPolicy attribute with a value of Delete to the S3 bucket.
Update the CloudFormation stack to add a DeletionPolicy attribute with a value of Snapshot for the S3 bucket resource.
Update the CloudFormation template to create an Amazon EFS file system to store temporary files instead of Amazon S3. Configure the Lambda functions to run in the same VPC as the EFS file system.

explanation:
CloudFormation cannot delete a bucket that is not empty. Add a Lambda-backed custom resource that empties the bucket when the
stack is deleted, and use DependsOn so it runs before the bucket deletion. No architecture changes are needed.
wrongOptionsExplanation:
B. Delete is already the default, and it does not empty the bucket. C. Snapshot is not a valid policy for S3 and would not empty it
either. D. Switching to EFS is a major architecture change.
plainWords: Deleting an old stack failed because the S3 bucket still contains objects.
keyPoints:
• Non-empty S3 bucket blocks stack delete = custom resource that empties it.
Reference: AWS documentation — https://docs.aws.amazon.com/

stem: A company has an application that stores user-uploaded videos in an Amazon S3 bucket using S3 Standard storage. Users access videos frequently for the first 180 days, and rarely after that. Most videos are over 100 MB. Users often have poor internet connectivity, and the company uses multipart uploads. A solutions architect needs tooptimize S3 storage costs. Which combination of actions will meet these requirements? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Configure the S3 bucket to be a Requester Pays bucket.
Use S3 Transfer Acceleration to upload the videos.
Create a lifecycle rule to expireincomplete multipart uploadsafter 7 days.
Create a lifecycle rule to transition objects toS3 Glacier Instant Retrieval after 1 day.
Create a lifecycle rule to transition objects toS3 Standard-IA after 180 days.

explanation:
Expire incomplete multipart uploads after 7 days (C) and transition to Standard-IA after 180 days (E). See Question 32 for the full
reasoning.
wrongOptionsExplanation:
A. Requester Pays does not work for anonymous users. B. Transfer Acceleration adds cost. D. Glacier Instant Retrieval after 1 day
causes retrieval charges while the data is still hot.
plainWords: This repeats Question 32: hot data for 180 days, then rare access, with failed multipart uploads.
keyPoints:
• Abort incomplete multipart uploads, and move to IA only when access really drops.
Reference: AWS documentation — https://docs.aws.amazon.com/

stem: A company is using an organization in AWS organization to manage AWS accounts. For each new project the company creates a new linked account. After the creation of a new account, the root user signs in to the new account and creates a service request to increase the service quota for Amazon EC2 instances. A solutions architect needs to automate this process. Which solution will meet these requirements with tie LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Create an Amazon EventBridge rule to detect creation of a new account Send the event to an Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) topic that invokes an AWS Lambda function. Configure the Lambda function to run the request-service-quota-increase command to request a service quota increase for EC2 instances.
Create a Service Quotas request template in the management account. Configure the desired service quota increases for EC2 instances.
Create an AWS Config rule in the management account to set the service quota for EC2 instances.

Create an Amazon EventBridge rule to detect creation of a new account. Send the event to an Amazon simple Notification service (Amazon SNS) topic that involves an AWS Lambda function. Configure the Lambda function to run the create-case command to request a service quota increase for EC2 instances.

wrongOptionsExplanation:
A. An EventBridge, SNS and Lambda pipeline that calls request-service-quota-increase works but is custom code to build and
maintain. C. AWS Config rules evaluate configuration and cannot set service quotas. D. The create-case command opens a Support
case, which is manual and not the Service Quotas API.
plainWords:
Each new account needs an EC2 quota increase, and a person currently logs in as root to request it. Automate with the least
overhead. Why my answer (B) works A Service Quotas request template in the management account applies the chosen quota
increases automatically to new accounts that join or are created in the organization. It is a built-in feature with no custom code to
maintain.
keyPoints:
• Automatic quota requests for new org accounts = Service Quotas request template.
HEADS-UP ON THIS QUESTION
• The bank key is A. The same feature appears in Question 81 as the intended solution, and it has the least overhead. Remember to
enable template association. I recommend B.
Reference: AWS documentation — https://docs.aws.amazon.com/

stem: A company runs AWS workloads that are integrated with software as a service (SaaS) applications. The company needs to analyze the SaaS applications to identify unused licenses. Which solution will meet this requirement with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Use AWS License Manager automated discovery to retrieve audit logs from the SaaS applications. Use Amazon Athena to analyze the data and to identify unused SaaS licenses.
Create an AWS Lambda function to retrieve audit logs from the SaaS applications and to store the data in Amazon S3. Use Amazon EMR to analyze the data and to identify unused SaaS licenses.
Use AWS AppFabric to ingest audit logs from the SaaS applications into Amazon S3. Use Amazon Athena to analyze the data and to identify unused SaaS licenses.
Use AWS App Runner to ingest audit logs from the SaaS applications into Amazon S3. Use Amazon EMR to analyze the data and to identify unused SaaS licenses.

explanation:
AWS AppFabric connects to SaaS applications, ingests their audit logs, normalizes them and delivers them to S3. Amazon Athena
then queries the data to find users who are not using their licenses.
wrongOptionsExplanation:
A. License Manager manages software licenses for AWS and on-prem workloads, not SaaS audit logs. B. Custom Lambda collectors
and EMR analysis are a lot of code and cluster work. D. App Runner runs web apps. It is not a log ingestion service.
plainWords: Analyze SaaS applications to identify unused licenses, with the least operational work.
keyPoints:
• SaaS audit log ingestion = AWS AppFabric; ad hoc analysis = Athena.
Reference: AWS documentation — https://docs.aws.amazon.com/

stem: A company is running a two-tier web-based application in an on-premises data center. The application layer consists of a single server running a stateful application. The application connects to a PostgreSQL database running on a separate server. The application’s user base is expected to grow significantly, so the company is migrating the application and database to AWS. The solution will use Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL, Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling, and Elastic Load Balancing. Which solution will provide a consistent user experience that will allow the application and database tiers to scale?

options.text: Enable Aurora Auto Scaling for Aurora Replicas. Use a Network Load Balancer with the least outstanding requests routing algorithm and sticky sessions enabled.
Enable Aurora Auto Scaling for Aurora writers. Use an Application Load Balancer with the round robin routing algorithm and sticky sessions enabled.
Enable Aurora Auto Scaling for Aurora Replicas. Use an Application Load Balancer with the round robin routing and sticky sessions enabled.
Enable Aurora Scaling for Aurora writers. Use a Network Load Balancer with the least outstanding requests routing algorithm and sticky sessions enabled.

explanation:
Aurora Auto Scaling adds and removes Aurora Replicas to scale reads. A stateful app needs sticky sessions so a user keeps talking to
the same server, and ALB supports cookie-based stickiness. Round robin with stickiness spreads new sessions evenly.
wrongOptionsExplanation:
A. NLB does not support cookie-based sticky sessions or least outstanding requests like the ALB. B. Aurora Auto Scaling scales
replicas, not writers. D. Both the writer scaling and NLB choices are wrong.
plainWords:
A stateful two-tier app moves to Aurora PostgreSQL with Auto Scaling and a load balancer. Users must get a consistent experience as
both tiers scale.
keyPoints:
• Aurora Auto Scaling = replicas. Stateful web tier = ALB with sticky sessions (or make the app stateless).
Reference: AWS documentation — https://docs.aws.amazon.com/

stem: A financial company needs to create a separate AWS account for a new digital wallet application. The company uses AWS Organizations to manage its accounts. A solutions architect uses the 1AM user Supportl from the management account to create a new member account with finance1@example.com as the email address. What should the solutions architect do to create IAM users in the new member account?

options.text: Sign in to the AWS Management Console with AWS account root user credentials by using the 64-character password from the initial AWS Organizations email senttofinance1@example.com. Set up the IAM users as required.
From the management account, switch roles to assume the OrganizationAccountAccessRole role with the account ID of the new member account. Set up the IAM users as required.

Go to the AWS Management Console sign-in page. Choose "Sign in using root account credentials." Sign in in by using the email address finance1@example.com and the management account's root password. Set up the IAM users as required.
Go to the AWS Management Console sign-in page. Sign in by using the account ID of the new member account and the Supportl IAM credentials. Set up the IAM users as required.

wrongOptionsExplanation:
A. No initial root password is sent by email. You would have to use "forgot password" to set one, and root should not be used for daily
work. C. The management account's root password does not work in member accounts. D. The IAM user Support1 exists only in the
management account, so it cannot sign in with the member account ID.
plainWords:
A management-account IAM user created a new member account. How do you create IAM users in it? Why my answer (B) works When
Organizations creates a member account it automatically creates the role OrganizationAccountAccessRole, which trusts the
management account. From the management account, switch role into that role using the member account ID and manage IAM there
(the IAM user needs permission to assume the role).
keyPoints:
• Member account created by Organizations = switch role to OrganizationAccountAccessRole.
HEADS-UP ON THIS QUESTION
• The bank key says D, but an IAM user from the management account does not exist in the member account, so it cannot sign in
there. B is the standard answer.
Reference: AWS documentation — https://docs.aws.amazon.com/

stem: A solutions architect needs to review the design of an Amazon EMR cluster that is using the EMR File System (EMRFS). The cluster performs tasks that are critical to business needs. The cluster is running Amazon EC2 On-Demand Instances at all times tor all task, primary, and core nodes. The EMR tasks run each morning, starting at 1 ;00 AM. and take 6 hours to finish running. The amount of time to complete the processing is not a priority because the data is not referenced until late in the day. The solutions architect must review the architecture and suggest a solution to minimize the compute costs. Which solution should the solutions architect recommend to meet these requirements?

options.text: Launch all task, primary, and core nodes on Spool Instances in an instance fleet. Terminate the cluster, including all instances, when the processing is completed.

Launch the primary and core nodes on On-Demand Instances. Launch the task nodes on Spot Instances in an instance fleet. Terminate the cluster, including all instances, when the processing is completed. Purchase Compute Savings Plans to cover the On-Demand Instance usage.

Continue to launch all nodes on On-Demand Instances. Terminate the cluster, including all instances, when the processing is completed. Purchase Compute Savings Plans to cover the On-Demand Instance usage

Launch the primary and core nodes on On-Demand Instances. Launch the task nodes on Spot Instances in an instance fleet. Terminate only the task node instances when the processing is completed. Purchase Compute Savings Plans to cover the On-Demand Instance usage.

explanation:
The data is in S3 through EMRFS, and the job is not time critical, so the cheapest design runs all nodes on Spot Instances in an
instance fleet (diversified types) and terminates the whole cluster after the job. You pay only for the hours used and at Spot prices.
wrongOptionsExplanation:
B. Keeping primary and core on On-Demand and buying Savings Plans costs more than Spot for a flexible job. C. All On-Demand is the
most expensive choice. D. Leaving primary and core nodes running after the job wastes money.
plainWords: An EMR cluster using EMRFS (data in S3) runs 6 hours nightly. Completion time is flexible, so minimize compute cost.
keyPoints:
• Flexible, restartable batch on S3 data = Spot + transient clusters. • EMRFS keeps data in S3, so losing nodes does not lose data.
HEADS-UP ON THIS QUESTION
• Using Spot for primary and core nodes risks the cluster failing mid-run. That is acceptable here because the job is restartable and
time is flexible.
Reference: AWS documentation — https://docs.aws.amazon.com/

stem: A company uses a single organization in AWS Organizations with all features enabled to manage 300 AWS accounts. A solutions architect must ensure that all private Amazon ECR repositories that are deployed in the member accounts are accessible only to principals that belong to the same organization. The company must enforce access controls across the entire organization and for all current and future ECR repositories. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Attach an SCP to the organization root that denies all ecr:* actions unless the aws:PrincipalType property has a value of Service.
Attach a resource control policy (RCP) to the organization root that allows access to ECR only when the aws:PrincipalOrgID condition matches the company’s organization ID.
Modify IAM policies across all accounts to include a deny statement for ecr:* unless the caller’s aws:PrincipalAccount property matches the organization’s ID.
Share all ECR repositories through AWS Resource Access Manager (AWS RAM). Control principal access based on account-level allowlists.

explanation:
A resource control policy (RCP) attached to the root sets the maximum permissions on resources in all member accounts. Using the
aws:PrincipalOrgID condition, ECR repositories can only be accessed by principals from your organization, including repositories
created later.
wrongOptionsExplanation:
A. An SCP restricts what your principals can do, not who from outside can access your resources, and denying ecr:* breaks normal
use. C. Editing IAM policies in 300 accounts is manual, and aws:PrincipalAccount is not an organization ID. D. RAM does not share ECR
repositories this way and allowlists are high maintenance.
plainWords:
Across 300 accounts, all private ECR repositories must be accessible only to principals in the same organization, now and in the
future.
keyPoints:
• Control access TO resources org-wide = RCP. Control what your principals can do = SCP.
Reference: AWS documentation — https://docs.aws.amazon.com/

stem: A company has VPC flow logs enabled for its NAT gateway. The company is seeing Action = ACCEPT for inbound traffic that comes from public IP address 198.51.100.2 destined for a private Amazon EC2 instance. A solutions architect must determine whether the traffic represents unsolicited inbound connections from the internet. The first two octets of the VPC CIDR block are 203.0. Which set of steps should the solutions architect take to meet these requirements?

options.text: Open the AWS CloudTrail console. Select the log group that contains the NAT gateway's elastic network interface and the private instance's elastic network interface. Run a query to filter with the destination address set as "like 203.0" and the source address set as "like 198.51.100.2". Run the stats command to filter the sum of bytes transferred by the source address and the destination address.

Open the Amazon CloudWatch console. Select the log group that contains the NAT gateway's elastic network interface and the private instance's elastic network interface. Run a query to filter with the destination address set as "like 203.0" and the source address set as "like 198.51.100.2". Run the stats command to filter the sum of bytes transferred by the source address and the destination address.

Open the AWS CloudTrail console. Select the log group that contains the NAT gateway's elastic network interface and the private instance's elastic network interface. Run a query to filter with the destination address set as "like 198.51.100.2" and the source address set as "like 203.0". Run the stats command to filter the sum of bytes transferred by the source address and the destination address.

Open the Amazon CloudWatch console. Select the log group that contains the NAT gateway's elastic network interface and the private instance's elastic network interface. Run a query to filter with the destination address set as "like 198.51.100.2" and the source address set as "like 203.0". Run the stats command to filter the sum of bytes transferred by the source address and the destination address.

explanation:
Flow logs are stored in CloudWatch Logs, so use CloudWatch Logs Insights (CloudTrail logs API calls, not network flows). Look for flows
where the private instance (203.0.x.x) is the source and 198.51.100.2 is the destination. If the instance first connected out to that
address, the inbound ACCEPT is just return traffic.
wrongOptionsExplanation:
A. CloudTrail does not hold flow logs, and the source and destination filters are reversed. B. Right service, but the source and
destination are reversed, so it looks for inbound requests, not outbound connections. C. Wrong service and the filter would not help.
plainWords:
Flow logs on a NAT gateway show ACCEPT for inbound traffic from 198.51.100.2 to a private instance. Is this an unsolicited inbound
connection or a reply?
keyPoints:
• VPC Flow Logs in CloudWatch Logs = query with Logs Insights. • To decide if inbound ACCEPT is a reply, look for the earlier
outbound flow.
Reference: AWS documentation — https://docs.aws.amazon.com/

stem: A company is migrating mobile banking applications to run on Amazon EC2 instances in a VPC. Backend service applications run in an on-premises data center. The data center has an AWS Direct Connect connection into AWS. The applications that run in the VPC need to resolve DNS requests to an on-premises Active Directory domain that runs in the data center. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST administrative overhead?

options.text: Provision a set of EC2 instances across two Availability Zones in the VPC as caching DNS servers to resolve DNS queries from the application servers within the VPC.
Provision an Amazon Route 53 private hosted zone. Configure NS records that point to on-premises DNS servers.
Create DNS endpoints by using Amazon Route 53 Resolver Add conditional forwarding rules to resolve DNS namespaces between the on-premises data center and the VPC.
Provision a new Active Directory domain controller in the VPC with a bidirectional trust between this new domain and the on-premises Active Directory domain.

explanation:
Create a Route 53 Resolver outbound endpoint and a forwarding rule for the AD domain pointing to the on-prem DNS servers. It is
managed and highly available, with no servers to run.
wrongOptionsExplanation:
A. Self-managed caching DNS servers on EC2 require patching and scaling. B. A private hosted zone with NS records to on-prem does
not delegate resolution that way. D. Running a new domain controller and trust is far more administration.
plainWords: EC2 apps in a VPC must resolve DNS names in an on-prem Active Directory domain over Direct Connect, with the least administration.
keyPoints:
• VPC to on-prem DNS = Route 53 Resolver outbound endpoint + forwarding rule.
Reference: AWS documentation — https://docs.aws.amazon.com/

stem: A company needs to migrate its on-premises database fleet to Amazon RDS. The company is currently using a mixture of Microsoft SQL Server, and Oracle databases. Some of the databases have custom schemas and stored procedures. Which combination of steps should the company take for the migration? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Use Migration Evaluator Quick Insights to analyze the source databases and to identify the stored procedures that need to be migrated.
Use AWS Application Migration Service to analyze the source databases and to identify the stored procedures that need to be migrated.
Use AWS SCT to analyze the source databases for changes that are required.
Use AWS DM5 to migrate the source databases to Amazon RD5.
Use AWS DataSync to migrate the data from the source databases to Amazon RDS.

wrongOptionsExplanation:
A. Migration Evaluator estimates cost, it does not analyze stored procedures. B. Application Migration Service rehosts servers and
does not analyze databases. E. DataSync transfers files, not database contents.
plainWords:
Migrate a mix of SQL Server and Oracle databases with custom schemas and stored procedures to RDS. Why my answer (C, D) works
AWS Schema Conversion Tool analyzes the source databases and shows what must change (C). AWS Database Migration Service then
moves the data (D), with ongoing replication if needed.
keyPoints:
• Database migration = SCT assessment + DMS data movement.
HEADS-UP ON THIS QUESTION
• The question says select two, but the bank key lists only C. The pair that fits is C and D.
Reference: AWS documentation — https://docs.aws.amazon.com/

stem: A company deploys an AI agent on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime. The agent processes customer requests. Some agent actions are classified as high risk and must receive human approval before proceeding. The workflow must pause the agent, notify a human approver, and resume or cancel the action based on the approver's decision. Approvals typically take between 5 minutes and 60 minutes. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Configure the agent to write high-risk action requests to an Amazon SQS queue. Create a separate polling application that reads the queue and sends approval email messages by using Amazon SES. Configure the application to invoke the agent by providing the approval result.

Configure an AWS Step Functions workflow that invokes the agent. Use a task token callback pattern to pause the workflow when the agent identifies a high-risk action. Send the task token to an approver by using Amazon SNS. Resume or cancel the workflow when the approver responds with the task token.

Configure the agent to invoke an AWS Lambda function for high-risk actions. Configure the Lambda function to send an approval email message by using Amazon SNS. Configure the Lambda function to poll an Amazon DynamoDB table until the approver updates the approval status.

Configure an Amazon EventBridge rule that intercepts all agent actions. Route high-risk actions to a separate approval queue. Create a second agent that monitors the queue and automatically approves or rejects actions without human input based on predefined rules.

explanation:
A Step Functions workflow with the task token callback pattern pauses at a task until something returns the token. Send the token to
the approver (for example by SNS or email link), and when they approve or reject, the workflow resumes or cancels. Standard
workflows can wait for very long periods at no extra cost.
wrongOptionsExplanation:
A. A custom polling application and manual re-invocation is more to build. C. A Lambda that polls DynamoDB for up to an hour is
wasteful and hits Lambda time limits. D. Automatic approval by a second agent removes the human the requirement demands.
plainWords:
An agent must pause before high-risk actions, notify a human, and resume or cancel based on the answer, with waits of 5 to 60
minutes.
keyPoints:
• Human-in-the-loop with long waits = Step Functions waitForTaskToken.
Reference: AWS documentation — https://docs.aws.amazon.com/

stem: A company runs a serverless application in a single AWS Region. The application accesses external URLs and extracts metadata from those sites. An Amazon SNS topic publishes URLs to an Amazon SQS queue. An AWS Lambda function processes messages from the queue and saves results to an Amazon S3 bucket. The company now needs to process each URL from additional AWS Regions to compare differences in website localization. URLs must continue to be published from the existing Region, and results must be saved to the existing S3 bucket. Which TWO changes meet these requirements? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Deploy an SQS queue with the Lambda function to other Regions.
Subscribe the SNS topic in each Region to the SQS queue.
Subscribe the SQS queue in each Region to the existing SNS topic in the original Region.
Configure the SQS queue to publish URLs to SNS topics in each Region.
Deploy the SNS topic and the Lambda function to other Regions.

explanation: Corrected study version: A deploys each regional SQS queue and Lambda consumer; C subscribes each regional queue to the single original-Region SNS topic. SNS supports cross-Region delivery to SQS, and each regional Lambda writes results to the original S3 bucket. B reverses SNS/SQS subscription direction; D assumes SQS publishes to SNS; E unnecessarily deploys regional SNS publishers.
wrongOptionsExplanation:
B. This direction is reversed: topics do not subscribe to queues. D. SQS queues do not publish to SNS topics. E. Extra SNS topics in
other Regions would not automatically receive the URLs published in the original Region.
plainWords:
URLs are published from one Region. The same URLs must also be processed in other Regions, and results must still go to the existing
S3 bucket.
keyPoints:
• SNS can fan out to SQS queues in other Regions.
HEADS-UP ON THIS QUESTION
• Option C is worded a little loosely in your PDF. The intended design is one topic in the original Region with queues in every Region
subscribed to it.
Reference: AWS documentation — https://docs.aws.amazon.com/
sourceWarning: A+C are intended, but C says SNS topics in each Region while the stem requires a single original-Region publisher. Correct design subscribes each regional SQS queue to the original SNS topic.

review.auditNote: Original stem and choices retained in originalQuestionSnapshot; A and C are corrected study options.

The company uses an Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) topic to publish URLs to an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue An AWS Lambda function uses the queue as an event source and processes the URLs from the queue Results are saved to an Amazon S3 bucket The company wants to process each URL other Regions to compare possible differences in site localization URLs must be published from the existing Region. Results must be written to the existing S3 bucket in the current Region. Which combination of changes will produce multi-Region deployment that meets these requirements? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Deploy the SOS queue with the Lambda function to other Regions.
Subscribe the SNS topic in each Region to the SQS queue.
Subscribe the SQS queue in each Region to the SNS topics in each Region.
Configure the SQS queue to publish URLs to SNS topics in each Region.
Deploy the SNS topic and the Lambda function to other Regions.

stem: A health insurance company stores personally identifiable information (PII) in an Amazon S3 bucket. The company uses server-side encryption with S3 managed encryption keys (SSE-S3) to encrypt the objects. According to a new requirement, all current and future objects in the S3 bucket must be encrypted by keys that the company’s security team manages. The S3 bucket does not have versioning enabled. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: In the S3 bucket properties, change the default encryption to SSE-S3 with a customer managed key. Use the AWS CLI to re-upload all objects in the S3 bucket. Set an S3 bucket policy to deny unencrypted PutObject requests.

In the S3 bucket properties, change the default encryption to server-side encryption with AWS KMS managed encryption keys (SSE-KMS). Set an S3 bucket policy to deny unencrypted PutObject requests. Use the AWS CLI to re-upload all objects in the S3 bucket.

In the S3 bucket properties, change the default encryption to server-side encryption with AWS KMS managed encryption keys (SSE-KMS). Set an S3 bucket policy to automatically encrypt objects on GetObject and PutObject requests.

In the S3 bucket properties, change the default encryption to AES-256 with a customer managed key. Attach a policy to deny unencrypted PutObject requests to any entities that access the S3 bucket. Use the AWS CLI to re-upload all objects in the S3 bucket.

explanation: DISPUTED QUESTION. The security team must control the encryption key for all existing and future objects. SSE-S3 (AES256) uses S3-managed keys, so A is wrong. B is the closest design because SSE-KMS can use a customer-managed KMS key, default encryption handles future uploads, and existing objects must be rewritten; however B does not explicitly require selecting a customer-managed KMS key. C neither re-encrypts existing objects nor correctly describes bucket policy behavior. D incorrectly combines AES256/default bucket encryption with a customer-managed key; SSE-C customer-provided keys cannot be configured as S3 bucket default encryption. No fully correct option as written. The original D is retained for audit traceability, NOT endorsed. CURRENT AWS UPDATE: Amazon S3 also documents UpdateObjectEncryption to change existing SSE-S3 objects to SSE-KMS without data movement; this does not make any original choice fully correct. A proper solution must explicitly configure a customer-managed KMS key.
wrongOptionsExplanation:
A. "SSE-S3 with a customer managed key" does not exist. SSE-S3 keys are managed by S3. C. A bucket policy cannot automatically
encrypt on GetObject or PutObject. Existing objects also stay on SSE-S3 until re-written. D. "AES-256 with a customer managed key"
is not a valid S3 option. AES-256 is the SSE-S3 setting.
plainWords:
All current and future objects must be encrypted with keys managed by the security team. The bucket currently uses SSE-S3 and has
no versioning. Why my answer (B) works Change the bucket default encryption to SSE-KMS using a customer managed KMS key (the
security team controls it), add a bucket policy that denies PutObject requests that do not use it, and re-copy the existing objects so
they are re-encrypted with the new key.
keyPoints:
• Keys managed by you in S3 = SSE-KMS with a customer managed key (or SSE-C). • Changing default encryption does not touch
existing objects. You must re-copy them.
HEADS-UP ON THIS QUESTION
• The bank key says D, but "AES-256 with a customer managed key" is not a real S3 configuration. B is the closest valid answer if it
uses a customer managed KMS key.
Reference: AWS documentation — https://docs.aws.amazon.com/
sourceWarning: Source key D invalid (AES256 means SSE-S3). B does not explicitly specify a customer managed KMS key. No option unambiguously satisfies requirement; original key retained pending original-source review.

review.auditNote: No fully correct original option. Updated AWS documentation additionally supports UpdateObjectEncryption for changing existing SSE-S3 objects to SSE-KMS without copying; the original question's suggested re-upload is not the only method. AES256 default does not support a KMS customer-managed key.
review.answerReason: External sites disagree: FreeCram B; FreePDFDumps and Certsmania D. SSE-C uses AES256 with customer-provided keys but cannot be configured as S3 bucket default encryption; SSE-KMS supports customer-managed KMS keys but B does not explicitly name customer-managed rather than AWS-managed KMS key. Retain D only as source key and mark ambiguous.

wrongOptionsReason.A: SSE-S3 keys are not customer managed.
wrongOptionsReason.B: Closest but unspecified KMS key defaults to AWS-managed aws/s3, not a security-team-controlled key.
wrongOptionsReason.C: Existing objects remain unchanged; GetObject does not perform re-encryption.
wrongOptionsReason.D: AES256 denotes SSE-S3 for bucket default encryption; cannot specify customer-managed key there.

review.suggestedCorrectedOptionB: Configure S3 bucket default encryption as SSE-KMS with a security-team-controlled customer managed KMS key. Re-encrypt existing objects using UpdateObjectEncryption or an appropriate S3 Batch Operations copy, and enforce the designated key for future uploads using a bucket policy.

stem: A company needs to establish a connection from its on-premises data center to AWS. The company needs to connect all of its VPCs that are located in different AWS Regions with transitive routing capabilities between VPC networks. The company also must reduce network outbound traffic costs, increase bandwidth throughput, and provide a consistent network experience for end users. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Create an AWS Site-to-Site VPN connection between the on-premises data center and a new central VPC. Create VPC peering connections that initiate from the central VPC to all other VPCs.

Create an AWS Direct Connect connection between the on-premises data center and AWS. Provision a transit VIF, and connect it to a Direct Connect gateway. Connect the Direct Connect gateway to all the other VPCs by using a transit gateway in each Region.
Create an AWS Site-to-Site VPN connection between the on-premises data centerand a new central VPC. Use a transit gateway with dynamic routing. Connect the transit gateway to all other VPCs.

Create an AWS Direct Connect connection between the on-premises data center and AWS Establish an AWS Site-to-Site VPN connection between all VPCs in each Region. Create VPC peering connections that initiate from the central VPC to all other VPCs.

explanation:
Direct Connect gives lower data-transfer-out cost, higher bandwidth and consistent latency. A transit VIF to a Direct Connect gateway
reaches Transit Gateways in multiple Regions, and each TGW fans out to its VPCs, giving transitive routing between on-prem and
VPCs.
wrongOptionsExplanation:
A. VPN is not consistent in performance, and VPC peering is not transitive. C. VPN over the internet does not reduce egress cost or
give consistent bandwidth. D. Mixing VPNs and peering between VPCs does not provide transitive routing.
plainWords:
Connect on-prem to many VPCs across Regions with transitive routing, lower egress cost, more bandwidth and consistent
performance.
keyPoints:
• Consistent, high bandwidth, lower egress = Direct Connect. Many VPCs and Regions = transit VIF + DX gateway + TGW.
HEADS-UP ON THIS QUESTION
• A Direct Connect gateway does not itself route traffic between the Transit Gateways attached to it. For VPC-to-VPC traffic across
Regions you would also peer the Transit Gateways.
Reference: AWS documentation — https://docs.aws.amazon.com/

stem: A solutions architect is investigating an issue in which a company cannot establish new sessions in Amazon Workspaces. An initial analysis indicates that the issue involves user profiles. The AmazonWorkspaces environment is configured to use Amazon FSx for Windows File Server as the profile share storage. The FSx for Windows File Server file system is configured with 10 TB of storage. The solutions architect discovers that the file system has reached its maximum capacity. The solutions architect must ensure that users can regain access. The solution also must prevent the problem from occurring again. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Remove old user profiles to create space. Migrate the user profiles to an Amazon FSx for Lustre file system.

Increase capacity by using the update-file-system command. Implement an Amazon CloudWatch metric that monitors free space. Use Amazon EventBridge to invoke an AWS Lambda function to increase capacity as required.
Monitor the file system by using the FreeStorageCapacity metric in Amazon CloudWatch. Use AWS Step Functions to increase the capacity as required.
Remove old user profiles to create space. Create an additional FSx for Windows File Server file system. Update the user profile redirection for 50% of the users to use the new file system.

explanation:
FSx for Windows lets you increase storage capacity online with the update-file-system command, which restores service. Then
monitor free space with CloudWatch (FreeStorageCapacity) and use EventBridge with a Lambda to raise capacity automatically
before it fills again.
wrongOptionsExplanation:
A. FSx for Lustre is not a Windows SMB profile store. C. Monitoring alone, with no action to fix the full file system, does not restore
access now. D. Splitting users across file systems by hand is manual and clumsy.
plainWords:
WorkSpaces users cannot start sessions because the FSx for Windows profile share (10 TB) is full. Restore access and prevent a
repeat.
keyPoints:
• FSx for Windows storage can only grow. Automate growth with CloudWatch + EventBridge + Lambda.
Reference: AWS documentation — https://docs.aws.amazon.com/

stem: A company runs a website on Amazon ECS containers that use the AWS Fargate launch type. The company configures AWS Application Auto Scaling by using a target tracking scaling policy. The company sets the request count as the scaling metric. An Application Load Balancer (ALB) serves traffic to the ECS containers. The website serves images on request and resizes the images to a predefined size to match the viewers' screens. After the website resizes an image, the website caches the image locally in a container and serves subsequent requests from the cache. During periods of high traffic, the company observed that images load slowly and with high latency. The company wants to minimize the latency to serve images. Which solution will meet this requirement with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Create a new Amazon CloudFront distribution and an Amazon S3 bucket. Set the ALB as one origin for the distribution and the S3 bucket as a second origin. Configure a cache behavior that routes image requests to the S3 origin, and configure a default cache behavior for the ALB origin. Pre-scale all images and upload the images to the S3 bucket.
Create an Amazon ElastiCache (Memcached) cluster. Update the application to read and write the resized images to the ElastiCache (Memcached) cluster by using the image name and size as the key.

Create an Amazon Aurora cluster and an Amazon S3 bucket. Update the application to store resized images in the S3 bucket and to store a cache key in the Aurora cluster. Configure the application to load the cache key from the Aurora cluster and to serve images from the S3 bucket.
Create an Amazon API Gateway HTTP API and enable API request caching. Replace the ALB with the HTTP API and remove the local caching in the application code.

explanation:
Store pre-sized images in S3 and serve them through CloudFront. The edge cache absorbs most requests, containers no longer resize
on the fly, and latency drops for every viewer. A cache behavior routes image paths to S3 and everything else to the ALB.
wrongOptionsExplanation:
B. ElastiCache works, but you must change and operate the application and cluster, and images are large for an in-memory cache. C.
Aurora to hold a cache key adds a database for no benefit. D. API Gateway caching in front of containers is not designed for large
image delivery and replaces the ALB for no reason.
plainWords:
Resized images are cached inside Fargate containers, so scaling spreads cache misses and latency is high. Reduce latency with
minimal operations.
keyPoints:
• Static or cacheable assets = CloudFront + S3.
HEADS-UP ON THIS QUESTION
• Pre-generating every image size takes up-front work. A related option is CloudFront with an on-demand resize function.
Reference: AWS documentation — https://docs.aws.amazon.com/

stem: A company manages hundreds of AWS accounts centrally in an organization in AWS Organizations. The company recently started to allow product teams to create and manage their own S3 access points in their accounts. The S3 access points can be accessed only within VPCs, not on the internet. What is the MOST operationally efficient way to enforce this requirement?

options.text: Set the S3 access point resource policy to deny the s3:CreateAccessPoint action unless the s3:AccessPointNetworkOrigin condition key evaluates to vpc.
Create an SCP at the root level in the organization to deny the s3:CreateAccessPoint action unless the s3:AccessPointNetworkOrigin condition key evaluates to VPC.
Use AWS CloudFormation StackSets to create a new IAM policy in each AWS account that allows the s3:CreateAccessPoint action only if the s3:AccessPointNetworkOrigin condition key evaluates to VPC.
Set the S3 bucket policy to deny the s3:CreateAccessPoint action unless the s3:AccessPointNetworkOrigin condition key evaluates to VPC.

explanation:
Attach an SCP at the root that denies s3:CreateAccessPoint unless the condition key s3:AccessPointNetworkOrigin equals VPC. It
applies to every current and future account automatically.
wrongOptionsExplanation:
A. A resource policy on the access point cannot control whether the access point can be created. C. Creating IAM policies with
StackSets still leaves teams able to bypass them with other permissions and needs upkeep. D. A bucket policy cannot deny creating
access points.
plainWords: Product teams may create S3 access points, but they must be VPC-only. Enforce this across hundreds of accounts efficiently.
keyPoints:
• Prevent creation of non-compliant resources org-wide = SCP with a service condition key.
Reference: AWS documentation — https://docs.aws.amazon.com/

stem: A company has an application that runs as a ReplicaSet of multiple pods in an Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) cluster. The EKS cluster has nodes in multiple Availability Zones. The application generates many small files that must be accessible across all running instances of the application. The company needs to back up the files and retain the backups for 1 year. Which solution will meet these requirements while providing the FASTEST storage performance?

options.text: Create an Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) file system and a mount target for each subnet that contains nodes in the EKS cluster. Configure the ReplicaSet to mount the file system. Direct the application to store files in the file system. Configure AWS Backup to back up and retain copies of the data for 1 year.

Create an Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) volume. Enable the EBS Multi- Attach feature. Configure the ReplicaSet to mount the EBS volume. Direct the application to store files inthe EBS volume. Configure AWS Backup to back up and retain copies of the data for 1 year.

Create an Amazon S3 bucket. Configure the ReplicaSet to mount the S3 bucket. Direct the application to store files in the S3 bucket. Configure S3 Versioning to retain copies of the data. Configure an S3 Lifecycle policy to delete objects after 1 year.
Configure the ReplicaSet to use the storage available on each of the running application pods to store the files locally. Use a third-party tool to back up the EKS cluster for 1 year.

explanation:
Amazon EFS is a shared POSIX file system across AZs and works with EKS pods, handling many small files. AWS Backup can retain
backups for one year with a simple backup plan.
wrongOptionsExplanation:
B. EBS Multi-Attach works only inside one AZ and for limited instances, and is not a shared file system for pods across AZs. C. S3 is
object storage and is not mounted as a fast POSIX file system for small files. D. Local pod storage disappears with the pod and cannot
be shared.
plainWords: Many small files must be accessible by all pods across AZs, with 1-year backups and the fastest suitable performance.
keyPoints:
• Shared file storage across AZs for Linux containers = EFS. Backups with retention = AWS Backup.
Reference: AWS documentation — https://docs.aws.amazon.com/

stem: A company runs many workloads on AWS and uses AWS Organizations to manage its accounts. The workloads are hosted on Amazon EC2. AWS Fargate. and AWS Lambda. Some of the workloads have unpredictable demand. Accounts record high usage in some months and low usage in other months. The company wants to optimize its compute costs over the next 3 years A solutions architect obtains a 6-month average for each of the accounts across the organization to calculate usage. Which solution will provide the MOST cost savings for all the organization's compute usage?

options.text: Purchase Reserved Instances for the organization to match the size and number of the most common EC2 instances from the member accounts.
Purchase a Compute Savings Plan for the organization from the management account by using the recommendation at the management account level
Purchase Reserved Instances for each member account that had high EC2 usage according to the data from the last 6 months.
Purchase an EC2 Instance Savings Plan for each member account from the management account based on EC2 usage data from the last 6 months.

review.note: Compute Savings Plans cover EC2, Fargate, and Lambda. Savings depend on a stable usage baseline.

stem: A company is migrating an application from on-premises infrastructure to the AWS Cloud. During migration design meetings, the company expressed concerns about the availability and recovery options for its legacy Windows file server. The file server contains sensitive business-critical data that cannot be recreated in the event of data corruption or data loss. According to compliance requirements, the data must not travel across the public internet. The company wants to move to AWS managed services where possible. The company decides to store the data in an Amazon FSx for Windows File Server file system. A solutions architect must design a solution that copies the data to another AWS Region for disaster recovery (DR) purposes. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Create a destination Amazon S3 bucket in the DR Region. Establish connectivity between the FSx for Windows File Server file system in the primary Region and the S3 bucket in the DR Region by using Amazon FSx File Gateway. Configure the S3 bucket as a continuous backup source in FSx File Gateway.

Create an FSx for Windows File Server file system in the DR Region. Establish connectivity between the VPC in the primary Region and the VPC in the DR Region by using AWS Site-to-Site VPN. Configure AWS DataSync to communicate by using VPN endpoints.

Create an FSx for Windows File Server file system in the DR Region. Establish connectivity between the VPC in the primary Region and the VPC in the DR Region by using VPC peering. Configure AWS DataSync to communicate by using interface VPC endpoints with AWS PrivateLink.

Create an FSx for Windows File Server file system in the DR Region. Establish connectivity between the VPC in the primary Region and the VPC in the DR Region by using AWS Transit Gateway in each Region. Use AWS Transfer Family to copy files between the FSx for Windows File Server file system in the primary Region and the FSx for Windows File Server file system in the DR Region over the private AWS backbone network.

explanation: Answer C (independently cross-checked with exact question copies on Freecram and Certstopics and with AWS documentation). Create FSx for Windows File Server in the DR Region, use inter-Region VPC peering for private connectivity, and use AWS DataSync to copy data and Windows metadata (including NTFS ACLs) to the DR file system. DataSync supports scheduled FSx-to-FSx cross-Region replication. The source option also specifies AWS PrivateLink interface VPC endpoints; these provide private DataSync agent-to-service connectivity where an agent is used, but modern same-account AWS-to-AWS FSx transfers generally do not require an agent or customer-managed interface endpoints. For production verify that the actual DataSync data path, service configuration, DNS, routing, security groups, Active Directory authentication, and backup/RPO requirements meet the no-public-internet rule. DataSync replication is periodic, not synchronous or a substitute for immutable backups.
wrongOptionsExplanation: A: Amazon FSx File Gateway is not a service that turns an FSx for Windows file system into an S3 continuous-backup source. B: Site-to-Site VPN and the stated 'VPN endpoints' are not the appropriate direct inter-Region VPC networking and DataSync configuration. C: Best answer: FSx in both Regions, VPC peering, and DataSync; PrivateLink detail is unnecessary for common agentless transfers. D: Inter-Region Transit Gateway connectivity is possible, but AWS Transfer Family is for managed file-transfer protocols, not purpose-built FSx-to-FSx replication; use DataSync.
plainWords: Copy sensitive Windows SMB file-server data from a primary AWS Region to a second Region for disaster recovery, without public-internet exposure.
keyPoints: C. FSx for Windows + AWS DataSync scheduled cross-Region copy + private VPC networking. Preserve NTFS permissions and metadata; validate RPO, backups and AD/DNS. Exact question and C key: https://www.freecram.net/question/Amazon.SAP-C02.v2024-03-21.q171/a-company-is-migrating-an-application-from-on-premises-infrastructure-to-the-aws-cloud-during-migration ; https://www.certstopics.com/questions/last-attempt-sap-c02-questions.html . AWS: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/fsx/latest/WindowsGuide/migrate-files-to-fsx-datasync.html ; https://aws.amazon.com/datasync/faqs/ ; https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/storage/how-to-replicate-amazon-fsx-file-server-data-across-aws-regions/ ; https://docs.aws.amazon.com/datasync/latest/userguide/do-i-need-datasync-agent.html
sourceWarning: The original C option explicitly mentions PrivateLink interface endpoints. That is a valid private endpoint pattern for DataSync agents but is not a universal requirement for modern agentless AWS-to-AWS FSx replication. Do not conflate PrivateLink control/service connectivity with SMB data transfer. The question's DR design also needs separate consideration of backup retention and recovery objectives.

review.status: Verified intended answer with implementation caveat
review.note: External question copies agree on C; AWS supports FSx cross-Region DataSync. PrivateLink endpoint detail is over-specific for agentless transfers.

stem: A company is running an event ticketing platform on AWS and wants to optimize the platform's cost-effectiveness. The platform is deployed on Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) with Amazon EC2 and is backed by an Amazon RDS for MySQL DB instance. The company is developing new application features to run on Amazon EKS with AWS Fargate. The platform experiences infrequent high peaks in demand. The surges in demand depend on event dates. Which solution will provide the MOST cost-effective setup for the platform?

options.text: Purchase Standard Reserved Instances for the EC2 instances that the EKS cluster uses in its baseline load. Scale the cluster with Spot Instances to handle peaks. Purchase 1-year All Upfront Reserved Instances for the database to meet predicted peak load for the year.

Purchase Compute Savings Plans for the predicted medium load of the EKS cluster. Scale the cluster with On-Demand Capacity Reservations based on event dates for peaks. Purchase 1-year No Upfront Reserved Instances for the database to meet the predicted base load. Temporarily scale out database read replicas during peaks.

Purchase EC2 Instance Savings Plans for the predicted base load of the EKS cluster. Scale the cluster with Spot Instances to handle peaks. Purchase 1-year All Upfront Reserved Instances for the database to meet the predicted base load. Temporarily scale up the DB instance manually during peaks.

Purchase Compute Savings Plans for the predicted base load of the EKS cluster. Scale the cluster with Spot Instances to handle peaks. Purchase 1-year All Upfront Reserved Instances for the database to meet the predicted base load. Temporarily scale up the DB instance manually during peaks.

explanation: SOURCE KEY B DISPUTED. The baseline should receive committed-use discounts, while short event-driven peaks are candidates for Spot where interruption tolerance allows. Compute Savings Plans cover both EC2 and EKS Fargate usage, unlike EC2 Instance Savings Plans. B commits to a medium rather than baseline load and uses On-Demand Capacity Reservations for peaks, which primarily guarantee capacity, not discounts; read replicas help only read-heavy DB load. D better matches the stated cost optimization pattern (baseline Compute Savings Plans, Spot peak capacity, baseline RDS RI, temporary DB scale-up), but manual database resizing and Spot interruption constraints mean the question cannot establish a universally cheapest answer without more information. Stored B retained pending external question match.
sourceWarning: B is source key, but On-Demand Capacity Reservations do not lower peak cost; D has Compute Savings Plans (also covers future Fargate), Spot peaks, and all-upfront baseline RDS RI. Cannot prove most cost-effective without workload assumptions; retain B pending comparison.

review.note: On-Demand Capacity Reservations guarantee capacity, not discounted pricing. Cheapest design depends on usage and workload assumptions.
review.auditNote: B is source key, but On-Demand Capacity Reservations do not lower peak cost; D has Compute Savings Plans (also covers future Fargate), Spot peaks, and all-upfront baseline RDS RI. Cannot prove most cost-effective without workload assumptions; retain B pending comparison.

wrongOptionsReason.A: Reserves database capacity for infrequent peak all year.
wrongOptionsReason.B: Source answer; reservations guarantee capacity rather than being a cost optimization for spikes; medium commitment may overcommit.
wrongOptionsReason.C: EC2 Instance Savings Plans do not cover Fargate usage.
wrongOptionsReason.D: Potentially better cost match, but manually scaling DB may require downtime and Spot may not suit all traffic.
