stem: A company maintains information on premises in approximately 1 million .csv files that are hosted on a VM. The data initially is 10 TB in size and grows at a rate of 1 TB each week. The company needs to automate backups of the data to the AWS Cloud. Backups of the data must occur daily. The company needs a solution that applies custom filters to back up only a subset of the data that is located in designated source directories. The company has set up an AWS Direct Connect connection. Which solution will meet the backup requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Use the Amazon S3 CopyObject API operation with multipart upload to copy the existing data to Amazon S3. Use the CopyObject API operation to replicate new data to Amazon S3 daily.
Create a backup plan in AWS Backup to back up the data to Amazon S3. Schedule the backup plan to run daily.
Install the AWS DataSync agent as a VM that runs on the on-premises hypervisor. Configure a DataSync task to replicate the data to Amazon S3 daily.
Use an AWS Snowball Edge device for the initial backup. Use AWS DataSync for incremental backups to Amazon S3 daily.

explanation: C is the independently AWS-documentation-supported answer. Install the AWS DataSync agent on an on-premises hypervisor, expose the VM-hosted CSV files via a supported NFS or SMB share, configure the on-premises source and S3 destination, use DataSync include/exclude filters to select directories, and schedule the task daily. DataSync can transfer changed files incrementally and verify transfers. The existing Direct Connect link can support private connectivity with correct endpoint/network configuration. For about 1 million files, consider Enhanced mode where supported or check Basic mode quotas. DataSync is a transfer/replication mechanism, not inherently a point-in-time versioned backup.
wrongOptionsExplanation: A: S3 CopyObject/UploadPartCopy copies objects already in S3, not on-premises VM files; custom upload and scheduling code adds overhead. B: AWS Backup plans do not directly back up an arbitrary on-premises VM filesystem to S3 with the stated DataSync-style directory filters; source type and integration are missing. C: Correct: DataSync agent + NFS/SMB source + S3 target + include/exclude filters + daily schedule + incremental changed-file transfers. D: Snowball Edge adds physical-device logistics for initial 10 TB despite Direct Connect, and is no longer available to new customers since November 7, 2025; daily DataSync still needed.
plainWords: Use DataSync to copy selected folders from an on-premises NFS/SMB share into S3 every day, sending only changed files after the initial transfer.
keyPoints: DataSync supports NFS/SMB-to-S3, on-premises agent, include/exclude directory filters, daily task scheduling, changed-file transfers, verification. S3 CopyObject is S3-to-S3. AWS Backup is not generic on-prem file share backup. DataSync replication is not immutable historical backup; use S3 Versioning/retention as appropriate. Snowball Edge closed to new customers Nov 7, 2025. Enhanced task mode can handle virtually unlimited files; Basic has object-count quotas.
sourceWarning: MODERATE: The stem says files are 'hosted on a VM' without specifying an NFS/SMB share; DataSync requires a supported source protocol and appropriate access. 'Backups' should not be confused with point-in-time recovery: configure S3 Versioning/Object Lock/retention if needed. Check Basic vs Enhanced mode for 1 million files. D is additionally outdated: Snowball Edge is not available to new customers from November 7, 2025. External exact-stem exam-site match or conflicting Choose TWO/THREE variant not independently found; AWS primary documentation verifies C.

review.notes: Domain 4 81/139. Q401 skipped (Select THREE). Original C independently verified against AWS documentation. No confirmed exact-stem external exam-site copy or conflicting multi-answer version. Caveats: NFS/SMB source must be exposed, DataSync is not retention backup, Basic-mode quotas, Snowball Edge new-customer availability.

stem: A company is running a workload that consists of thousands of Amazon EC2 instances. The workload is running in a VPC that contains several public subnets and private subnets. The public subnets have a route for 0.0.0.0/0 to an existing internet gateway. The private subnets have a route for 0.0.0.0/0 to an existing NAT gateway. A solutions architect needs to migrate the entire fleet of EC2 instances to use IPv6. The EC2 instances that are in private subnets must not be accessible from the public internet. What should the solutions architect do to meet these requirements?

options.text: Update the existing VPC, and associate a custom IPv6 CIDR block with the VPC and all subnets. Update all the VPC route tables, and add a route for ::/0 to the internet gateway.

Update the existing VPC, and associate an Amazon-provided IPv6 CIDR block with the VPC and all subnets. Update the VPC route tables for all private subnets, and add a route for ::/0 to the NAT gateway.

Update the existing VPC, and associate an Amazon-provided IPv6 CIDR block with the VPC and all subnets. Create an egress-only internet gateway. Update the VPC route tables for all private subnets, and add a route for ::/0 to the egress-only internet gateway.

Update the existing VPC, and associate a custom IPv6 CIDR block with the VPC and all subnets. Create a new NAT gateway, and enable IPv6 support. Update the VPC route tables for all private subnets, and add a route for ::/0 to the IPv6-enabled NAT gateway.

stem: A company provides a software as a service (SaaS) application that runs in the AWS Cloud. The application runs on Amazon EC2 instances behind a Network LoadBalancer (NLB). The instances are in an Auto Scaling group and are distributed across three Availability Zones in a single AWS Region. The company is deploying the application into additional Regions. The company must provide static IP addresses for the application to customers so that the customers can add the IP addresses to allow lists. The solution must automatically route customers to the Region that is geographically closest to them. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Create an Amazon CloudFront distribution. Create a CloudFront origin group. Add the NLB for each additional Region to the origin group. Provide customers with the IP address ranges of the distribution's edge locations.
Create an AWS Global Accelerator standard accelerator. Create a standard accelerator endpoint for the NLB in each additional Region. Provide customers with the Global Accelerator IP address.
Create an Amazon CloudFront distribution. Create a custom origin for the NLB in each additional Region. Provide customers with the IP address ranges of the distribution's edge locations.

Create an AWS Global Accelerator custom routing accelerator. Create a listener for the custom routing accelerator. Add the IP address and ports for the NLB in each additional Region. Provide customers with the Global Accelerator IP address.

stem: A company runs an application on Amazon EC2 and AWS Lambda. The application stores temporary data in Amazon 53. The 53 objects are deleted after 24 hours. The company deploys new versions of the application by launching AWS CloudFormation stacks. The stacks create the required resources. After validating a new version, the company deletes the old stack. The deletion of an old development stack recently failed. A solutions architect needs to resolve this Issue without major architecture changes. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Create a Lambda function to delete objects from an 53 bucket. Add the Lambda function as acustom resource in the CloudFormation stack with a DependsOn attribute that points to the S3 bucket resource.
Modify the CkxidFormatton stack to attach a DeletionPolicy attribute with a value of Delete to the S3 bucket.
Update the CloudFormation stack to add a DeletionPolicy attribute with a value of Snapshot for the S3 bucket resource.
Update the CloudFormation template to create an Amazon EFS file system to store temporary files Instead of Amazon S3. Configure the Lambda functions to run in the same VPC as the EFS file system.

stem: A company is running a containerized workload on AWS. The workload consists of several data-processing services that run on a group of Amazon EC2 instances. The company uploads new data to an Amazon S3 bucket every night. A cron job on each EC2 instance starts the data processing every night. The amount of uploaded data varies. The data-processing tasks can take hours to finish running. After the data is processed, the services remain idle until the next processing window occurs the next night. The company needs a solution to modernize the architecture and reduce the operational overhead. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Migrate the workload to AWS Lambda functions that run the container images. Configure an Amazon EventBridge rule to filter S3 events and invoke the Lambda functions when data is uploaded to the S3 bucket.

Migrate the workload to run as tasks in an Amazon ECS cluster that runs on AWS Fargate. Create an AWS Step Functions state machine to invoke the Fargate tasks. Configure S3 Event Notifications to invoke the state machine tasks when data is uploaded to the S3 bucket.

Migrate the workload to run as tasks in an Amazon ECS cluster that runs on AWS Fargate. Create an AWS Step Functions state machine to invoke the Fargate tasks. Configure an Amazon EventBridge rule to invoke the state machine when data is uploaded to the S3 bucket.

Migrate the workload to AWS Lambda functions by packaging the container images as Lambda layers. Configure S3 Event Notifications to invoke the Lambda functions when data is uploaded to the S3 bucket.

explanation: C is correct for the specified services. S3 Object Created events can be delivered to Amazon EventBridge (when S3 EventBridge delivery is enabled); an EventBridge rule can start a Step Functions state machine; Step Functions can run ECS Fargate tasks with the ecs:runTask.sync integration and wait for long-running container work. Fargate removes always-on EC2 host management and charges for running tasks instead of idle hosts. The S3/EventBridge/Step Functions pattern is explicitly documented in AWS's Step Functions tutorial.
wrongOptionsExplanation: A: Standard AWS Lambda container-image functions have a 15-minute timeout; these jobs can take hours. B: S3 Event Notifications do not directly target a Step Functions state machine; an EventBridge rule is needed (or another intermediary). C: Correct: S3 EventBridge notifications -> EventBridge rule -> Step Functions -> ECS Fargate tasks; works for hours-long processing without idle EC2 hosts. D: Lambda layers are ZIP dependency archives, not container-image packaging; standard Lambda execution time is also too short.
plainWords: Trigger a Step Functions workflow when nightly files arrive in S3, run the existing processing containers on Fargate, and stop them when processing finishes.
keyPoints: S3 EventBridge delivery must be enabled; EventBridge rules can start Step Functions; Step Functions ecs:runTask.sync waits for ECS/Fargate completion; Fargate removes EC2 host management. Standard Lambda functions time out after 15 minutes; container images cannot be packaged as Lambda layers. Multiple S3 events may start duplicate or premature workflows without a batch-completion signal.
sourceWarning: MODERATE AMBIGUITY: 'when data is uploaded' could trigger one execution per S3 Object Created event, potentially starting processing before the nightly batch is complete. Add an upload-completion marker, aggregation, or idempotency if one nightly run is required. S3-to-EventBridge delivery must be explicitly enabled. AWS documents a distinct Lambda Managed Instances mode with longer timeouts; ordinary Lambda container-image functions described in A/D remain unsuitable. No independently confirmed exact-stem external exam site or conflicting Choose TWO/THREE variant in available search results.

review.notes: Domain 4 82/139; Q410–Q412 outside Domain 4. Official AWS docs validate C. External exact-stem single/multiple-answer variant not independently established. C requires S3 EventBridge enabled; account for multiple events and nightly batch completion. Distinguish standard Lambda 15m limit from newer Managed Instances mode.

stem: A company runs an application in an on-premises data center. The application gives users the ability to upload media files. The files persist in a file server. The web application has many users. The application server is overutilized, which causes data uploads to fail occasionally. The company frequently adds new storage to the file server. The company wants to resolve these challenges by migrating the application to AWS. Users from across the United States and Canada access the application. Only authenticated users should have the ability to access the application to upload files. The company will consider a solution that refactors the application, and the company needs to accelerate application development. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Use AWS Application Migration Service to migrate the application server to Amazon EC2 instances. Create an Auto Scaling group for the EC2 instances. Use an Application Load Balancer to distribute the requests. Modify the application to use Amazon S3 to persist the files. Use Amazon Cognito to authenticate users.

Use AWS Application Migration Service to migrate the application server to Amazon EC2 instances. Create an Auto Scaling group for the EC2 instances. Use an Application Load Balancer to distribute the requests. Set up AWS IAM Identity Center (AWS Single Sign-On) to give users the ability to sign in to the application. Modify the application to use Amazon S3 to persist the files.

Create a static website for uploads of media files. Store the static assets in Amazon S3. Use AWS AppSync to create an API. Use AWS Lambda resolvers to upload the media files to Amazon S3. Use Amazon Cognito to authenticate users.

Use AWS Amplify to create a static website for uploads of media files. Use Amplify Hosting to serve the website through Amazon CloudFront. Use Amazon S3 to store the uploaded media files. Use Amazon Cognito to authenticate users.

explanation: D is correct. AWS Amplify accelerates development and deployment of a static upload frontend. Amplify Hosting uses Amazon CloudFront to deliver website assets across North America; Amazon Cognito authenticates users; Amplify Storage supports direct authorized browser uploads to Amazon S3, avoiding the overloaded on-premises application server and fixed file-server capacity. AWS documentation and an AWS Storage Blog architecture corroborate this combination. Exact-stem SAP-C02 exam sites examsvce and examtopics.cn both key D as a single-answer item.
wrongOptionsExplanation: A: EC2 Auto Scaling, ALB, S3 and Cognito could work but preserve EC2 infrastructure and management overhead despite permitted refactoring. B: Same EC2/ALB operational burden, and IAM Identity Center is primarily workforce access rather than the best fit for a public customer-facing upload application. C: Static S3 frontend, AppSync, Lambda and Cognito can be engineered, but adds GraphQL API/resolver complexity and potentially proxies file payloads through Lambda; direct S3 uploads with Amplify are simpler. D: Correct: Amplify static frontend and Hosting/CloudFront CDN, Cognito user authentication, S3 storage and direct upload capabilities minimize operational overhead.
plainWords: Replace the overloaded upload server with a static Amplify website, use Cognito sign-in, and send media directly from users' browsers to S3.
keyPoints: Amplify Hosting serves frontend assets through CloudFront. Amplify Storage supports direct uploads to S3. Cognito provides end-user sign-in. S3 removes fixed file-server capacity. IAM Identity Center focuses on workforce access. AppSync/Lambda resolvers add unnecessary API complexity for basic file uploads. CloudFront distribution of the website does not itself accelerate S3 upload traffic.
sourceWarning: LOW: Original stem typo 'usersshould' corrected to 'users should'. Enforce authorized S3 upload access via Cognito-linked credentials/permissions, bucket policies and object prefixes. CloudFront CDN is for hosting assets and does not by itself guarantee accelerated S3 uploads. Exact-stem external sources examsvce and examtopics.cn both key D, single answer; no verified Choose TWO/THREE variant.

review.notes: Domain 4 83/139. Correct D verified against AWS documentation and two exact-stem external exam sites; both single answer. Corrected source typo 'usersshould'. Cognito/S3 upload authorization and CloudFront vs S3 upload path caveats.

stem: A company uses AWS Organizations. The company creates a central VPC in an AWS account that is designated for networking in a single AWS Region. The central VPC has an AWS Site-to-Site VPN connection to the company's on-premises network. A solutions architect must create another AWS account that uses the same networking resources that the central VPC uses. Which solution meets these requirements MOST cost-effectively?

options.text: Create a VPC in the new AWS account. Create a new Site-to-Site VPN connection for the on-premises connection.
Use AWS Resource Access Manager to share the VPN connection in the central VPC with the new AWS account.
Create a VPC in the new AWS account. Configure a virtual private gateway to connect to the central VPC.
Use AWS Resource Access Manager to share the subnets in the central VPC with the new AWS account.

stem: A company migrated an application to the AWS Cloud. The application runs on two Amazon EC2 instances behind an Application Load Balancer (ALB). Application data is stored in a MySQL database that runs on an additional EC2 instance. The application's use of the database is read-heavy. The application loads static content from Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) volumes that are attached to each EC2 instance. The static content is updated frequently and must be copied to each EBS volume. The load on the application changes throughout the day. During peak hours, the application cannot handle all the incoming requests. Trace data shows that the database cannot handle the read load during peak hours. Which solution will improve the reliability of the application?

options.text: Migrate the application to a set of AWS Lambda functions. Set the Lambda functions as targets for the ALB. Create a new single EBS volume for the static content. Configure the Lambda functions to read from the new EBS volume. Migrate the database to an Amazon RDS for MySQL Multi-AZ DB cluster.

Migrate the application to a set of AWS Step Functions state machines. Set the state machines as targets for the ALB. Create an Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) file system for the static content. Configure the state machines to read from the EFS file system. Migrate the database to Amazon Aurora MySQL Serverless v2 with a reader DB instance.

Containerize the application. Migrate the application to an Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) Cluster. Use the AWS Fargate launch type for the tasks that host the application. Create a new single EBS volume for the static content. Mount the new EBS volume on the ECS cluster. Configure AWS Application Auto Scaling on ECS cluster. Set the ECS service as a target for the ALB. Migrate the database to an Amazon RDS for MySQL Multi-AZ DB cluster.

Containerize the application. Migrate the application to an Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) cluster. Use the AWS Fargate launch type for the tasks that host the application. Create an Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) file system for the static content. Mount the EFS file system to each container. Configure AWS Application Auto Scaling on the ECS cluster. Set the ECS service as a target for the ALB. Migrate the database to Amazon Aurora MySQL Serverless v2 with a reader DB instance.

explanation: D is correct: migrate the application to an ECS service using AWS Fargate with ECS Service Auto Scaling to handle changing HTTP demand, use Amazon EFS as a concurrently accessible shared file system for frequently updated static assets, and migrate the read-heavy MySQL database to Aurora MySQL Serverless v2 with a reader DB instance for elastic read scaling. The ECS service can be registered with the ALB using IP-type targets. AWS documentation confirms EFS shared access from Fargate and Aurora Serverless v2 reader scaling.
wrongOptionsExplanation: A: Lambda can be an ALB target and RDS MySQL Multi-AZ DB clusters can have readable standbys, but Lambda cannot mount an EBS volume as specified. B: Step Functions state machines are workflow orchestration resources, not ALB targets or compute instances that mount EFS. C: ECS Fargate scaling and an RDS MySQL Multi-AZ DB cluster with readable standbys are viable, but a single shared EBS volume is not a general concurrent shared filesystem for independently scaling Fargate tasks; task-attached EBS volumes are task-scoped. D: Correct: ECS Fargate auto scaling + shared EFS + Aurora Serverless v2 reader resolves application, content consistency, and read bottlenecks.
plainWords: Auto-scale the application containers on Fargate, share changing static files through EFS, and use a scalable Aurora database with a reader for heavy queries.
keyPoints: ECS Fargate service auto scaling; ALB IP targets for awsvpc tasks; EFS can be mounted by multiple Fargate tasks; Fargate EBS volumes are task-scoped, not a multi-task shared file system; Aurora Serverless v2 supports reader instances and elastic capacity; RDS for MySQL Multi-AZ DB clusters also offer readable standby instances; Step Functions cannot be direct ALB targets; Lambda cannot mount EBS.
sourceWarning: MODERATE: Corrected grammatical/typing defects in stem and options: 'The loads static content', 'EBSvolume', 'ECS duster', 'MySOL', missing 'for', and punctuation. RDS MySQL Multi-AZ DB cluster is not inherently unsuitable for reads; C fails on EBS sharing. Source external exam copy uses a different option order; map by content, not answer letter. Matching exact-stem external source is single-answer; no independently confirmed Choose TWO/THREE variant. Consider EFS throughput/latency and Aurora reader endpoint routing in implementation.

review.notes: Domain 4 84/139. Historical correct D validated independently against AWS docs. Exact-stem third-party copy found with reordered options; no confirmed Choose TWO/THREE variant. Fixed typos. Clarified that RDS Multi-AZ DB cluster supports readable standbys, so C fails because task-scoped EBS is not shared EFS.

stem: A company is launching a new online game on Amazon EC2 instances. The game must be available globally. The company plans to run the game in three AWS Regions: us-east-1, eu-west-1, and ap-southeast-1. The game's leaderboards. player inventory, and event status must be available across Regions. A solutions architect must design a solution that will give any Region the ability to scale to handle the load of all Regions. Additionally, users must automatically connect to the Region that provides the least latency. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Create an EC2 Spot Fleet. Attach the Spot Fleet to a Network Load Balancer (NLB) in each Region. Create an AWS Global Accelerator IP address that points to the NLB. Create an Amazon Route 53 latency-based routing entry for the Global Accelerator IP address. Save the game metadata to an Amazon RDS for MySQL DB instance in each Region. Set up a read replica in the other Regions.

Create an Auto Scaling group for the EC2 instances. Attach the Auto Scaling group to a Network Load Balancer (NLB) in each Region. For each Region, create an Amazon Route 53 entry that uses geoproximity routing and points to the NLB in that Region. Save the game metadata to MySQL databases on EC2 instances in each Region. Save the game metadata to MySQL databases on EC2 instances in each Region. Set up replication between the database EC2 instances in each Region.

Create an Auto Scaling group for the EC2 instances. Attach the Auto Scaling group to a Network Load Balancer (NLB) in each Region. For each Region, create an Amazon Route 53 entry that uses latency-based routing and points to the NLB in that Region. Save the game metadata to an Amazon DynamoDB global table.

Use EC2 Global View. Deploy the EC2 instances to each Region. Attach the instances to a Network Load Balancer (NLB). Deploy a DNS server on an EC2 instance in each Region. Set up custom logic on each DNS server to redirect the user to the Region that provides the lowest latency. Save the game metadata to an Amazon Aurora global database.

stem: A solutions architect is designing the data storage and retrieval architecture for a new application that a company will be launching soon. The application is designed to ingest millions of small records per minute from devices all around the world. Each record is less than 4 KB in size and needs to be stored in a durable location where it can be retrieved with low latency. The data is ephemeral and the company is required to store the data for 120 days only, after which the data can be deleted. The solutions architect calculates that, during the course of a year, the storage requirements would be about 10-15 TB. Which storage strategy is the MOST cost-effective and meets the design requirements?

options.text: Design the application to store each incoming record as a single .csv file in an Amazon S3 bucket to allow for indexed retrieval. Configure a lifecycle policy to delete data older than 120 days.

Design the application to store each incoming record in an Amazon DynamoDB table properly configured for the scale. Configure the DynamoOB Time to Live (TTL) feature to delete records older than 120 days.
Design the application to store each incoming record in a single table in an Amazon RDS MySQL database. Run a nightly cron job that executes a query to delete any records older than 120 days.

Design the application to batch incoming records before writing them to an Amazon S3 bucket. Update the metadata for the object to contain the list of records in the batch and use the Amazon S3 metadata search feature to retrieve the data. Configure a lifecycle policy to delete the data after 120 days.

stem: A company has purchased appliances from different vendors. The appliances all have loT sensors. The sensors send status information in the vendors' proprietary formats to a legacy application that parses the information into JSON. The parsing is simple, but each vendor has a unique format. Once daily, the application parses all the JSON records and stores the records in a relational database for analysis. The company needs to design a new data analysis solution that can deliver faster and optimize costs. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Connect the loT sensors to AWS loT Core. Set a rule to invoke an AWS Lambda function to parse the information and save a .csv file to Amazon S3. Use AWS Glue to catalog the files. Use Amazon Athena and Amazon OuickSight for analysis.

Migrate the application server to AWS Fargate, which will receive the information from loT sensors and parse the information into a relational format. Save the parsed information to Amazon Redshift for analysis.

Create an AWS Transfer for SFTP server. Update the loT sensor code to send the information as a .csv file through SFTP to the server. Use AWS Glue to catalog the files. Use Amazon Athena for analysis.
Use AWS Snowball Edge to collect data from the loT sensors directly to perform local analysis. Periodically collect the data into Amazon Redshift to perform global analysis.

stem: A company wants to migrate its data analytics environment from on premises to AWS. The environment consists of two simple Node.js applications. One application collects sensor data and loads it into a MySQL database. The other application aggregates the data into reports. When the aggregation jobs run, some of the load jobs fail to run correctly. The company must resolve the data loading issue. The company also needs the migration to occur without interruptions or changes for the company's customers. What should a solutions architect do to meet these requirements?

options.text: Set up an Amazon Aurora MySQL database as a replication target for the on-premises database. Create an Aurora Replica for the Aurora MySQL database, and move the aggregation jobs to run against the Aurora Replica. Set up collection endpoints as AWS Lambda functions behind a Network Load Balancer (NLB), and use Amazon RDS Proxy to write to the Aurora MySQL database. When the databases are synced, disable the replication job and restart the Aurora Replica as the primary instance. Point the collector DNS record to the NLB.

Set up an Amazon Aurora MySQL database. Use AWS Database Migration Service (AWS DMS) to perform continuous data replication from the on-premises database to Aurora. Move the aggregation jobs to run against the Aurora MySQL database. Set up collection endpoints behind an Application Load Balancer (ALB) as Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group. When the databases are synced, point the collector DNS record to the ALB. Disable the AWS DMS sync task after the cutover from on premises to AWS.

Set up an Amazon Aurora MySQL database. Use AWS Database Migration Service (AWS DMS) to perform continuous data replication from the on-premises database to Aurora. Create an Aurora Replica for the Aurora MySQL database and move the aggregation jobs to run against the Aurora Replica. Set up collection endpoints as AWS Lambda functions behind an Application Load Balancer (ALB), and use Amazon RDS Proxy to write to the Aurora MySQL database. When the databases are synced, point the collector DNS record to the ALB. Disable the AWS DMS sync task after the cutover from on premises to AWS.

Set up an Amazon Aurora MySQL database. Create an Aurora Replica for the Aurora MySQL database and move the aggregation jobs to run against the Aurora Replica. Set up collection endpoints as an Amazon Kinesis data stream. Use Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose to replicate the data to the Aurora MySQL database. When the databases are synced, disable the replication job and restart the Aurora Replica as the primary instance. Point the collector DNS record to the Kinesis data stream.

explanation: C is correct. AWS DMS full-load-plus-CDC continuously copies on-premises MySQL data into Aurora MySQL during migration, preserving the original service until controlled cutover. An Aurora reader instance and its reader endpoint isolate expensive aggregation SELECT queries from writer-side ingestion. ALB can target Lambda functions that implement the existing collection HTTP API; RDS Proxy pools database connections from concurrently executing Lambda functions. Once DMS lag reaches zero and writes are coordinated, repoint the existing collector DNS name to the ALB and stop CDC after successful cutover. This is a near-zero-downtime strategy, not a literal guarantee of zero interruption.
wrongOptionsExplanation: A: Network Load Balancer does not support Lambda targets directly (ALB does), and 'restart the Aurora Replica as primary' is not a valid standard cutover procedure. B: DMS/ALB/EC2 can migrate ingestion but reporting against the same Aurora writer does not isolate aggregation load, so contention can persist. C: Correct: DMS CDC + Aurora read replica for reports + ALB Lambda collector + RDS Proxy for pooled writes + DNS cutover. D: Kinesis data streams cannot simply replace the existing HTTP collection endpoint; Amazon Data Firehose does not have a direct Aurora MySQL delivery destination, and the replication/cutover design is unsupported.
plainWords: Keep the current MySQL system running while DMS copies it to Aurora, send heavy reports to an Aurora reader, and move sensor collection to Lambda behind the same DNS name using ALB and RDS Proxy.
keyPoints: DMS full-load + CDC supports low-downtime MySQL migration; monitor replication lag and coordinate final writes. Aurora reader endpoint offloads reporting SELECT queries. ALB supports Lambda target groups; NLB does not. RDS Proxy manages Lambda-to-Aurora connections. DNS repointing does not ensure absolutely zero disruption. Data Firehose does not directly deliver to Aurora MySQL.
sourceWarning: MODERATE: Repaired extensive punctuation/OCR defects in stem/options without changing technical intent. 'Without interruptions' is overly absolute: DMS CDC has variable replication lag; final write quiescence, validation, DNS TTL and client connection behavior must be planned. Exact-stem third-party practice site presents C as a single-answer question; no independently confirmed Choose TWO/THREE variant. Original option A's 'restart Aurora Replica as primary' is technically misleading.

review.notes: Domain 4 85/139. AWS docs validate DMS CDC, Aurora read endpoint, Lambda/RDS Proxy and ALB. Exact-stem external SPOTO Q58 keys C, single-answer; Pupuweb same stem. No confirmed Choose TWO/THREE variant. Corrected OCR typos and flagged near-zero vs zero downtime.

stem: How should EC2 instances in AWS synchronize their clocks with an on-premises atomic clock NTP server, with the least administrative overhead?

options.text: Configure a DHCP options set with the on-prem NTP server.
Use a custom AMI with Amazon Time Sync.
Deploy a 3rd-party NTP server from Marketplace.
Create an IPsec VPN tunnel to sync over Direct Connect.

explanation: A is correct. An Amazon VPC DHCP options set supports the ntp-servers setting for on-premises NTP IP addresses. Associate the custom option set with the VPC, permit NTP UDP/123 over existing Direct Connect routing, and ensure the EC2 guest OS actually honors the DHCP NTP setting. This is a compressed duplicate of Q386, which presents the full scenario and same four solutions. AWS primary documentation verifies this behavior; third-party exact-stem longer variants also key the DHCP answer.
wrongOptionsExplanation: A: Correct: centrally distribute the on-premises NTP server address through VPC DHCP options, subject to OS configuration and network reachability. B: Amazon Time Sync at 169.254.169.123 uses AWS's time source, not the required on-premises atomic clock. C: Third-party Marketplace NTP relay adds an unnecessary managed appliance. D: An IPsec VPN adds complexity and does not configure NTP clients; Direct Connect already provides connectivity if routing and firewalls allow UDP/123.
plainWords: Point the VPC DHCP NTP setting to the company's existing atomic-clock-backed NTP server so EC2 instances can synchronize with it.
keyPoints: Confirmed duplicate/abbreviated variant of Q386 (Domain 4 position 79/139). VPC DHCP option ntp-servers supports custom NTP server IP addresses. Direct Connect needs routing and UDP/123 reachability. EC2 guest chrony/ntpd/Windows Time must apply the setting. AWS Time Sync is a different time source. An external practice explanation wrongly favors AWS Time Sync despite the on-premises-source requirement.
sourceWarning: DUPLICATE OF Q386 — not a distinct SAP-C02 study topic. Fixed 'on-premisesatomic' and 'theleast' spacing defects. Exact-stem full variants are single-answer; no independently confirmed Choose TWO/THREE variant. One external exam site includes a conflicting rationale favoring AWS Time Sync; reject it based on the on-premises-clock requirement and AWS DHCP documentation. Stratum-0 atomic reference typically feeds a stratum-1 NTP server; OS client adoption must be verified. Additional external discrepancy: ExamsLabs rearranges the option letters and lists A for an Amazon Time Sync AMI despite DHCP being labeled C; its keyed answer contradicts the requirement for the on-premises atomic reference. Prefer solution content over the site's letter. Verified full-stem single-answer copies at solution2pass, DumpsMate, and FreeCram all favor the DHCP option.

review.notes: Domain 4 86/139. Confirmed abbreviated duplicate of Q386, same solution choices and answer A. External full-stem sources single-answer, no confirmed Choose TWO/THREE variant. stem: A global media company is planning a multi-Region deployment of an application. Amazon DynamoDB global tables will back the deployment to keep the user experience consistent across the two continents where users are concentrated. Each deployment will have a public Application Load Balancer (ALB). The company manages public DNS internally. The company wants to make the application available through an apex domain. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST effort?

options.text: Migrate public DNS to Amazon Route 53. Create CNAME records for the apex domain to point to the ALB. Use a geolocation routing policy to route traffic based on user location.

Place a Network Load Balancer (NLB) in front of the ALB. Migrate public DNS to Amazon Route 53. Create a CNAME record for the apex domain to point to the NLB's static IP address. Use a geolocation routing policy to route traffic based on user location.

Create an AWS Global Accelerator accelerator with multiple endpoint groups that target endpoints in appropriate AWS Regions. Use the accelerator's static IP address to create a record in public DNS for the apex domain.

Create an Amazon API Gateway API that is backed by AWS Lambda in one of the AWS Regions. Configure a Lambda function to route traffic to application deployments by using the round robin method. Create CNAME records for the apex domain to point to the API's URL.

explanation: C is correct. AWS Global Accelerator provides two static anycast IPv4 addresses by default and supports ALBs as regional endpoints. Create a standard accelerator, listener and endpoint groups for each Region, attach the existing public ALBs, then create apex-domain A records in the existing authoritative DNS pointing to both accelerator IP addresses. Global Accelerator routes to healthy regional endpoints without DNS migration or an extra proxy tier.
wrongOptionsExplanation: A: Invalid: standard CNAME records cannot be placed at the zone apex; Route 53 alias A/AAAA records could point to ALBs but are not what the option says and require migrating DNS. B: Invalid: a CNAME cannot target a literal NLB IP address and cannot be used at the apex; extra NLBs and DNS migration add effort. C: Correct: static Global Accelerator IP addresses support apex A records and regional ALB endpoints, retaining existing DNS. D: Invalid: apex CNAME limitation remains, and API Gateway plus Lambda round-robin routing adds complexity and a single-Region routing dependency.
plainWords: Keep the company's existing DNS. Point the root domain's A records to AWS Global Accelerator's static IP addresses, and connect the accelerator to the ALBs in both Regions.
keyPoints: Apex/root domains cannot use ordinary CNAME records. Global Accelerator allocates two IPv4 addresses by default; publish both as A records. A standard accelerator supports ALB endpoints and regional health-aware traffic distribution. Route 53 alias records are a different valid apex-domain mechanism, but not offered correctly here. No independently verified Choose TWO/THREE variant.
sourceWarning: Original options B and D contain invalid DNS constructions; B attempts CNAME to an IP address and apex CNAME; A and D attempt apex CNAME. External sites reorder option letters, so compare the Global Accelerator solution content, not letter. The wording 'static IP address' is singular, while standard IPv4 Global Accelerator allocates two; configure A records for both. DynamoDB global tables do not by themselves guarantee strong cross-Region consistency. No confirmed multi-answer variant.

review.notes: Domain 4 87/139; full-stem single-answer verified. FreeCram and Pupuweb key C; PassTest reorders and keys A, same Global Accelerator solution. No confirmed Choose TWO/THREE variant. Correct answer C; record apex-CNAME and singular-IP defects.

stem: A company has many services running in its on-premises data center. The data center is connected to AWS using AWS Direct Connect (DX) and an IPsec VPN. The service data is sensitive and connectivity cannot traverse the internet. The company wants to expand to a new market segment and begin offering its services to other companies that are using AWS. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Create a VPC Endpoint Service that accepts TCP traffic, host it behind a Network Load Balancer, and make the service available over DX.
Create a VPC Endpoint Service that accepts HTTP or HTTPS traffic, host it behind an Application Load Balancer, and make the service available over DX.
Attach an internet gateway to the VPC, and ensure that network access control and security group rules allow the relevant inbound and outbound traffic.
Attach a NAT gateway to the VPC, and ensure that network access control and security group rules allow the relevant inbound and outbound traffic.

explanation: A is correct. AWS PrivateLink endpoint services are backed by a Network Load Balancer (or Gateway Load Balancer), not a standalone Application Load Balancer. Create a TCP NLB in the provider VPC with IP targets reachable on premises over Direct Connect/VPN; publish it as an endpoint service and grant customer AWS principals access. Customers create interface VPC endpoints, keeping connectivity private.
wrongOptionsExplanation: A: Correct: NLB-backed PrivateLink endpoint service supports TCP and private customer access; on-prem IP targets require supported routing and health checks. B: Incorrect: an ALB cannot be attached directly as a PrivateLink endpoint-service load balancer, although an ALB may sit behind an NLB. C: Incorrect: an internet gateway creates public internet exposure and violates the requirement. D: Incorrect: NAT gateway supports outbound translation, not publishing a private endpoint service to customers.
plainWords: Put an NLB in AWS in front of the on-premises services, publish an AWS PrivateLink endpoint service, and allow customer VPCs to connect privately.
keyPoints: PrivateLink endpoint service requires NLB or GWLB. NLB can forward TCP to on-premises IP targets over hybrid connectivity when target IPs are supported and reachable. Interface endpoints allow cross-account private consumption. ALB alone is not a valid endpoint-service backing load balancer.
sourceWarning: CORRECTED WRONG SOURCE KEY B -> A. Source option B incorrectly asserts an ALB can directly back a VPC endpoint service. Source has OCR defects: 'DX)and', 'interne', 'Is services', 'ensue'. The phrase 'make service available over DX' is shorthand: Direct Connect links provider AWS VPC to on-prem targets, while customers access via PrivateLink endpoints. Exact-stem external PDF confirms four-option single-answer presentation, but answer key should not supersede AWS primary docs; no confirmed Choose TWO/THREE variant.

review.notes: Domain 4 88/139. Primary AWS docs mandate NLB or GWLB for endpoint service; B (ALB alone) invalid. Correct to A. External exact-stem PDF displays single-answer four-choice format; no independently confirmed multi-answer variant.

stem: A company needs to architect a hybrid DNS solution. This solution will use an Amazon Route 53 private hosted zone for the domain cloud.example.com for the resources stored within VPCs. The company has the following DNS resolution requirements: • On-premises systems should be able to resolve and connect to cloud.example.com. • All VPCs should be able to resolve cloud.example.com. Associate the private hosted zone to all the VPCs. Deploy an Amazon EC2 conditional forwarder in the shared services VPC. Attach all VPCs to the transit gateway and create forwarding rules in the on-premises DNS server for cloud.example.com that point to the conditional forwarder.

Associate the private hosted zone to the shared services VPC. Create a Route 53 outbound resolver in the shared services VPC. Attach all VPCs to the transit gateway and create forwarding rules in the on-premises DNS server for cloud.example.com that point to the outbound resolver.

stem: A company runs a Python script on an Amazon EC2 instance to process data. The script runs every 10 minutes. The script ingests files from an Amazon S3 bucket and processes the files. On average, the script takes approximately 5 minutes to process each file. The script will not reprocess a file that the script has already processed. The company reviewed Amazon CloudWatch metrics and noticed that the EC2 instance is idle for approximately 40% of the time because of the file processing speed. The company wants to make the workload highly available and scalable. The company also wants to reduce long-term management overhead. Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?

options.text: Migrate the data processing script to an AWS Lambda function. Use an S3 event notification to invoke the Lambda function to process the objects when the company uploads the objects.

Create an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue. Configure Amazon S3 to send event notifications to the SQS queue. Create an EC2 Auto Scaling group with a minimum size of one instance. Update the data processing script to poll the SQS queue. Process the S3 objects that the SQS message identifies.

Migrate the data processing script to a container image. Run the data processing container on an EC2 instance. Configure the container to poll the S3 bucket for new objects and to process the resulting objects.

Migrate the data processing script to a container image that runs on Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) on AWS Fargate. Create an AWS Lambda function that calls the Fargate RunTaskAPI operation when the container processes the file. Use an S3 event notification to invoke the Lambda function.

explanation: A is correct. S3 ObjectCreated event notifications invoke Lambda asynchronously for each new file, eliminating periodic EC2 polling and idle capacity. The five-minute average processing time is within Lambda's 15-minute maximum. Lambda provides managed scaling and usage-based pricing, reducing operational overhead compared with EC2 and ECS. Confirm worst-case runtime, memory, temporary storage, and concurrency; handle duplicate S3 notifications with idempotency.
wrongOptionsExplanation: A: Correct. Direct S3-to-Lambda events provide serverless, event-driven processing with no always-on EC2 capacity. B: S3 to SQS to EC2 Auto Scaling is feasible but minimum one EC2 instance remains running and requires OS, scaling and worker management. C: EC2-hosted container still needs always-on EC2, polling and HA operations. D: Fargate adds ECS task startup and operational complexity for jobs Lambda can handle; wording says invoke RunTask when the container processes the file, reversing the required invocation sequence.
plainWords: Trigger the existing Python processing logic as a Lambda function whenever a new file lands in S3; stop paying for an idle EC2 worker.
keyPoints: Lambda supports 15-minute maximum execution, sufficient for five-minute average but verify worst case. S3 ObjectCreated notifications can directly invoke Lambda. S3 event notifications are at least once and can be out of order, so implement idempotency. Set appropriate memory, timeout and concurrency. Watch for recursive triggers if output is written to same bucket.
sourceWarning: MINOR: Corrected missing period after 'each file'. Average processing time alone does not guarantee all jobs fit Lambda's 15-minute limit. At-least-once S3 notifications require duplicate handling. Option D reverses RunTask invocation order. External SPOTO keys A; Brainscape flashcard keys D despite the stated Lambda-suitable workload, an external answer conflict. Exact-stem four-option single-answer versions found; no confirmed Choose TWO/THREE variant.

review.notes: Domain 4 89/139. AWS supports direct S3 Lambda notifications and five-minute average fits 15-minute Lambda maximum. SPOTO keys A; Brainscape flashcard claims D, but D unnecessarily adds Fargate and has reversed RunTask timing. No confirmed multi-answer variant.

stem: A retail company wants to improve its application architecture. The company's applications register new orders, handle returns of merchandise, and provide analytics. The applications store retail data in a MySQL database and an Oracle OLAP analytics database. All the applications and databases are hosted on Amazon EC2 instances. Each application consists of several components that handle different parts of the order process. These components use incoming data from different sources. A separate ETL job runs every week and copies data from each application to the analytics database. A solutions architect must redesign the architecture into an event-driven solution that uses serverless services. The solution must provide updated analytics in near real time. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Migrate the individual applications as microservices to Amazon ECS containers that use AWS Fargate. Keep the retail MySQL database on Amazon EC2. Move the analytics database to Amazon Neptune. Use Amazon SQS to send all the incoming data to the microservices and the analytics database.

Create an Auto Scaling group for each application. Specify the necessary number of EC2 instances in each Auto Scaling group. Migrate the retail MySQL database and the analytics database to Amazon Aurora MySQL. Use Amazon SNS to send all the incoming data to the correct EC2 instances and the analytics database.

Migrate the individual applications as microservices to Amazon EKS containers that use AWS Fargate. Migrate the retail MySQL database to Amazon Aurora Serverless MySQL. Migrate the analytics database to Amazon Redshift Serverless. Use Amazon EventBridge to send all the incoming data to the microservices and the analytics database.

Migrate the individual applications as microservices to Amazon AppStream 2.0. Migrate the retail MySQL database to Amazon Aurora MySQL. Migrate the analytics database to Amazon Redshift Serverless. Use AWS IoT Core to send all the incoming data to the microservices and the analytics database.

explanation: C is the best single answer. EKS pods on AWS Fargate provide serverless container compute; Aurora Serverless MySQL handles operational transactions; Redshift Serverless provides an analytics warehouse; and EventBridge routes application events to consumers. However, EventBridge alone does not automatically insert event payloads into Redshift Serverless tables. A compatible ingestion component or pipeline must load the data, and EKS still requires cluster administration.
wrongOptionsExplanation: A: Fargate microservices are suitable, but EC2-hosted MySQL is not serverless, and Neptune is a graph database rather than a general OLAP replacement. B: EC2 Auto Scaling groups are not serverless, and Aurora MySQL is not an appropriate substitute for a dedicated analytics warehouse. C: Best fit: Fargate, Aurora Serverless, Redshift Serverless, and EventBridge support event-driven serverless application and analytics architecture, subject to implementing ingestion into Redshift. D: AppStream 2.0 streams end-user desktop applications rather than backend microservices; IoT Core is not the general event bus for retail orders and returns.
plainWords: Move retail microservices to EKS on Fargate, transactions to Aurora Serverless, analytics to Redshift Serverless, and distribute business events with EventBridge plus an actual warehouse ingestion pipeline.
keyPoints: EventBridge routes application events near real time but does not itself load Redshift Serverless tables. Redshift Serverless is the OLAP warehouse. Aurora Serverless is the transactional MySQL-compatible store. EKS Fargate removes node management, not Kubernetes cluster operations. External exam sites reorder letters: ExamTopics C, PDFDumps D, same solution.
sourceWarning: MODERATE ARCHITECTURAL OMISSION: The option implies EventBridge directly sends all data to Redshift Serverless; a supported ingestion integration/consumer is needed for table inserts. EKS on Fargate still has Kubernetes operational overhead. External single-answer copies agree on architecture with reordered letters. No independently confirmed Choose TWO/THREE variant.

review.notes: Domain 4 90/139. ExamTopics answer C and PDFDumps answer D correspond to identical EKS Fargate + Aurora Serverless + Redshift Serverless + EventBridge solution. EventBridge is not automatic Redshift row ingestion. No confirmed Choose TWO/THREE variant.

stem: A company has an loT platform that runs in an on-premises environment. The platform consists of a server that connects to loT devices by using the MQTT protocol. The platform collects telemetry data from the devices at least once every 5 minutes The platform also stores device metadata in a MongoDB cluster An application that is installed on an on-premises machine runs periodic jobs to aggregate and transform the telemetry and device metadata The application creates reports that users view by using another web application that runs on the same on-premises machine The periodic jobs take 120-600 seconds to run However, the web application is always running. The company is moving the platform to AWS and must reduce the operational overhead of the stack. Which combination of steps will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead? (Select THREE.)

options.text: Use AWS Lambda functions to connect to the loT devices
Configure the loT devices to publish to AWS loT Core
Write the metadata to a self-managed MongoDB database on an Amazon EC2 instance
Write the metadata to Amazon DocumentDB (with MongoDB compatibility)
Use AWS Step Functions state machines with AWS Lambda tasks to prepare the reports and to write the reports to Amazon S3 Use Amazon CloudFront with an S3origin to serve the reports
Use an Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) cluster with Amazon EC2 instances to prepare the reports Use an ingress controller in the EKS cluster to serve the reports

explanation: Correct answers: B, D, E. B: AWS IoT Core is the managed MQTT broker/connectivity endpoint for device-published telemetry, replacing the on-premises MQTT server. D: Amazon DocumentDB (with MongoDB compatibility) provides a managed document database for device metadata, eliminating self-managed MongoDB operations (validate application API and aggregation compatibility before cutover). E: Step Functions orchestrates Lambda-based periodic report generation; S3 stores generated static reports and CloudFront distributes them, avoiding always-on report/web EC2 and EKS infrastructure. Historical 120–600-second jobs fit within the standard Lambda 900-second limit when configured and profiled, assuming no individual execution exceeds 900 seconds. AWS IoT rules and/or integration are additionally needed to route telemetry to processing/storage, and a periodic EventBridge Scheduler schedule may trigger the workflow.
wrongOptionsExplanation: A: Incorrect. A Lambda function is not a persistent managed MQTT broker/connection fleet and Lambda layers are not a durable message buffer. B: Correct. AWS IoT Core handles managed MQTT device ingestion; its rules route messages into processing/storage. C: Incorrect. Hosting MongoDB on EC2 leaves patching, backups, availability, upgrades and database operations to the company. D: Correct. DocumentDB reduces database administration, subject to MongoDB API/feature compatibility checks. E: Correct. Step Functions+Lambda prepares reports, while S3+CloudFront replace continuously running report web servers for static reports. F: Incorrect. EC2-backed EKS plus an ingress controller entails cluster, nodes, Kubernetes and networking management unnecessary for these short periodic jobs and static reports.
plainWords: Replace the three on-premises components with managed services: IoT devices publish MQTT to IoT Core; metadata moves from MongoDB to DocumentDB; short report jobs use Step Functions/Lambda and reports are served from S3 through CloudFront.
keyPoints: Select THREE B,D,E. IoT Core supports MQTT 3.1.1/5.0 with QoS 0/1, not QoS 2. IoT Rules can invoke Lambda/route to S3 etc.; a direct DocumentDB IoT Rules action is not implied. AWS Lambda standard timeout is configurable up to 900 seconds (15 minutes); 120–600 seconds can fit but reserve margin. For scheduled reporting use EventBridge Scheduler to start Step Functions. CloudFront S3 origin with Origin Access Control (OAC) protects private reports; use viewer authorization/signed URLs/cookies if confidential. Amazon DocumentDB does not support every MongoDB feature; test compatibility/migration. Q116 is a scenario-level near-duplicate with reordered A,D,E answers, NOT a disagreement with Q438 B,D,E.
sourceWarning: SOURCE OCR/PUNCTUATION: 'loT' vs IoT, 'S3origin', missing sentence boundaries; preserve stem/options for provenance. ARCHITECTURE GAPS: Option B does not describe IoT Rules downstream routing; option E does not state the trigger or authentication and presumes report-viewing site is static. Potential long-tail job durations must fit applicable Lambda timeout. DocumentDB compatibility is not feature-identical to MongoDB. Exact external Q438 mirrors (Exact2Pass/Pupuweb/Pass2Lead) show B,D,E; independently researched reworded Q116 external mirrors (CertsHero/Certstopics/ExamTopics) show A,D,E because of reordered choices plus IoT rule detail, not a conflicting architecture. Exam mirrors may copy shared source, not independent AWS authority. BANK DUPLICATE: Q116 strong conceptual near-duplicate; no other equivalent full-stack duplicate; related Q228/Q255/Q467/Q509/Q583 IoT messaging, Q258/Q453 MongoDB-to-DocumentDB, Q420 and Q434 serverless/reporting. Q467 stored key A is suspicious given managed AWS IoT Core option B; separately audit Q467. stem: A company is migrating its on-premises file transfer solution to AWS Transfer Family. The on-premises host includes an SFTP server to receive files, an application that performs a transformation of the files, and a messaging server. The transformations run every 5 minutes. When a transformation is complete, the application sends a message to a queue on the messaging server. The company needs to simplify the solution and reduce the management of the components. What should the company do to meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Configure Transfer Family to use Amazon EFS storage. Use a cron job on Amazon EFS to perform the transformations. Configure the cron job to publish a message to an Amazon SNS topic when a file has been transformed.
Configure Transfer Family to use Amazon S3 storage. Use Amazon EMR to perform the transformations. Configure Amazon EMR to send a message to an Amazon SNS topic when a file has been transformed.

Configure Transfer Family to use Amazon S3 storage. Use AWS Glue to perform the transformations after S3 event notifications. Configure AWS Glue to send a message to an Amazon SQS queue when a file has been transformed.

Configure Transfer Family to use Amazon EFS storage. Create an AWS Glue time- based job to run every 5 minutes to initiate an AWS Glue transformation. Configure AWS Glue to send a message to an Amazon SQS queue when a file has been transformed.

explanation: C is the best answer. AWS Transfer Family receives SFTP uploads into S3. S3 object-created events can be routed through EventBridge to an AWS Glue workflow or trigger, replacing the fixed five-minute polling schedule. Glue transforms uploaded data, and job code or a success-state event consumer sends an SQS completion message. These managed services eliminate self-managed SFTP, transformation hosts, and messaging servers. S3 event notifications do not automatically run Glue without the trigger integration.
wrongOptionsExplanation: A: Incorrect: Amazon EFS is storage and cannot execute a cron job; a compute host would be required. SNS is pub/sub rather than a queue replacement. B: Incorrect: EMR is unnecessarily complex for this managed event-driven file-processing use case, and SNS is not a direct replacement for a durable SQS work queue. C: Correct: Transfer Family + S3 + event-triggered Glue + SQS minimizes component administration while preserving queued completion messages. D: Incorrect: EFS with a scheduled Glue job retains time-based polling and adds unnecessary storage integration complexity; event-driven S3 processing is more suitable.
plainWords: Upload SFTP files to S3 with Transfer Family, trigger Glue when a file arrives, and send an SQS message after transformation succeeds.
keyPoints: Transfer Family supports S3 and EFS. S3 notifications/EventBridge can initiate Glue workflows via configured triggers. Glue can emit job state changes; use job logic or EventBridge consumer to send SQS message on successful completion. EFS is not compute and cannot run cron. SNS pub/sub differs from SQS queue.
sourceWarning: MODERATE: Option C abbreviates the necessary S3 EventBridge-to-Glue trigger configuration and Glue-to-SQS completion publishing. S3 notifications alone do not directly execute a Glue job. Option A is technically invalid because cron cannot run on EFS. Exact-stem external practice sources key C as a single-answer question; no independently confirmed Choose TWO/THREE variant.

review.notes: Domain 4 91/139. Four external sources key C, single-answer; AWS primary docs support Transfer Family S3 and EventBridge Glue workflow triggers. No confirmed Choose TWO/THREE variant. Flag S3-to-Glue and Glue-to-SQS orchestration omissions.

Create an Amazon API Gateway HTTP API that implements the RESTful API. Create an Amazon SQS queue. Create an API Gateway service integration with the SQS queue. Create an AWS Lambda function to process messages in the SQS queue.

Create an Amazon API Gateway REST API that implements the RESTful API. Create a fleet of Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group. Create an API Gateway Auto Scaling group proxy integration. Use the EC2 instances to process incoming data.

Create an Amazon CloudFront distribution for the RESTful API. Create a data stream in Amazon Kinesis Data Streams. Set the data stream as the origin for the distribution. Create an AWS Lambda function to consume and process data in the data stream.

stem: A company has migrated a legacy application to the AWS Cloud. The application runs on three Amazon EC2 instances that are spread across three Availability Zones. One EC2 instance is in each Availability Zone. The EC2 instances are running in three private subnets of the VPC and are set up as targets for an Application Load Balancer (ALB) that is associated with three public subnets. The application needs to communicate with on-premises systems. Only traffic from IP addresses in the company's IP address range are allowed to access the on-premises systems. The company's security team is bringing only one IP address from its internal IP address range to the cloud. The company has added this IP address to the allow list for the company firewall. The company also has created an Elastic IP address for this IP address. A solutions architect needs to create a solution that gives the application the ability to communicate with the on-premises systems. The solution also must be able to mitigate failures automatically. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Deploy three NAT gateways, one in each public subnet. Assign the Elastic IP address to the NAT gateways. Turn on health checks for the NAT gateways. If a NAT gateway fails a health check, recreate the NAT gateway and assign the Elastic IP address to the new NAT gateway.

Replace the ALB with a Network Load Balancer (NLB). Assign the Elastic IP address to the NLB. Turn on health checks for the NLB. In the case of a failed health check, redeploy the NLB in different subnets.

Deploy a single NAT gateway in a public subnet. Assign the Elastic IP address to the NAT gateway. Use Amazon CloudWatch with a custom metric to monitor the NAT gateway. If the NAT gateway is unhealthy, invoke an AWS Lambda function to create a new NAT gateway in a different subnet. Assign the Elastic IP address to the new NAT gateway.

Assign the Elastic IP address to the ALB. Create an Amazon Route 53 simple record with the Elastic IP address as the value. Create a Route 53 health check. In the case of a failed health check, recreate the ALB in different subnets.

explanation: C is the intended legacy single-answer exam key, corroborated by Pass2Lead and FreeCram, but the scenario is architecturally ambiguous and cannot be considered unconditionally valid. A single zonal public NAT gateway can translate outbound private-subnet instance traffic to one EIP only when traffic egresses via an internet gateway. Custom CloudWatch alarm/Lambda orchestration could replace a failed zonal NAT gateway in another AZ, but must release/reassociate the EIP, update all affected subnet routes, and handle recovery races. Critically, AWS documents that traffic routed to on-premises via transit gateway/virtual private gateway uses the NAT gateway's PRIVATE IP as source, not its EIP. The question calls the allowlisted IP internal while calling it an EIP; the connectivity path is unspecified. Modern regional NAT gateways (introduced Nov 2025) change the best-practice design, but can use separate EIPs per AZ, conflicting with a strict single-EIP requirement.
wrongOptionsExplanation: A: Impossible to associate one EIP with three separate NAT gateways concurrently; NAT gateway health-check/recreation is not a built-in option as written. B: An NLB's static IP is for inbound listener connections; replacing the ALB does not provide outbound source NAT for EC2 traffic to on-premises systems. C: Intended exam answer for single fixed public egress IP with custom failover; requires EIP release, route table updates, connectivity path clarification, and is wrong if private DX/VPN routing expects EIP source. D: ALB does not support directly associating EIPs, and Route 53 health checks cannot implement outbound NAT.
plainWords: For the original public-egress exam interpretation, use one NAT gateway with a fixed EIP and automate failover. For private on-premises connectivity, the source address is the NAT gateway private IP instead; clarify routing before deployment.
keyPoints: EIP cannot be simultaneously attached to multiple NAT gateways. NLB is not outbound NAT. ALB cannot directly use an EIP. Public NAT gateway's EIP is used only via IGW; via TGW/VGW the private NAT address is used. Zonal NAT failover needs EIP reassignment and route updates. AWS added regional NAT gateways in Nov 2025, but multi-AZ EIP behavior may violate one-IP allowlisting.
sourceWarning: HIGH / DEFECTIVE AMBIGUOUS QUESTION. The source states an IP from internal range and also an Elastic IP, but these are not equivalent. No DX/VPN/IGW path specified; NAT EIP is not source over private TGW/VGW. C is intended legacy key, not guaranteed valid as written. External sites Pass2Lead/FreeCram key C; PUPUWEB keys B with technically false NLB outbound-SNAT explanation. Modern regional NAT gateway feature (Nov 2025) makes zonal-Lambda solution outdated for some use cases, but regional mode may use multiple EIPs. Minor OCR typo 'tomonitor' and NLB wording corrected. Checked copies single-choice, no confirmed Choose TWO/THREE variant.

review.notes: Domain 4 92/139. Retain intended source C with HIGH warning, not fully valid for private on-prem route. Pass2Lead and FreeCram C, PUPUWEB erroneous B. New regional NAT capability Nov 2025 noted. No confirmed multi-answer variant.

stem: A company hosts a data-processing application on Amazon EC2 instances. The application polls an Amazon Elastic File System (Amazon EFS) file system for newly uploaded files. When a new file is detected, the application extracts data from the file and runs logic to select a Docker container image to process the file. The application starts the appropriate container image and passes the file location as a parameter. The data processing that the container performs can take up to 2 hours. When the processing is complete, the code that runs inside the container writes the file back to Amazon EFS and exits. The company needs to refactor the application to eliminate the EC2 instances that are running the containers. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Create an Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) cluster. Configure the processing to run as AWS Fargate tasks. Extract the container selection logic to run as an Amazon EventBridge rule that starts the appropriate Fargate task. Configure the EventBridge rule to run when files are added to the EFS file system.

Create an Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) cluster. Configure the processing to run as AWS Fargate tasks. Update and containerize the container selection logic to run as a Fargate service that starts the appropriate Fargate task. Configure an EFS event notification to invoke the Fargate service when files are added to the EFS file system.

Create an Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) cluster. Configure the processing to run as AWS Fargate tasks. Extract the container selection logic to run as an AWS Lambda function that starts the appropriate Fargate task. Migrate the storage of file uploads to an Amazon S3 bucket. Update the processing code to use Amazon S3. Configure an S3 event notification to invoke the Lambda function when objects are created.

Create AWS Lambda container images for the processing. Configure Lambda functions to use the container images. Extract the container selection logic to run as a decision Lambda function that invokes the appropriate Lambda processing function. Migrate the storage of file uploads to an Amazon S3 bucket. Update the processing code to use Amazon S3. Configure an S3 event notification to invoke the decision Lambda function when objects are created.

explanation: C: S3 ObjectCreated notification invokes a Lambda dispatcher that selects the container and starts a long-running ECS Fargate task. Fargate supports two-hour processing. Lambda functions, including container-image Lambda, have a 15-minute maximum execution time.
wrongOptionsExplanation: A: EFS has no native file-created EventBridge rule. B: EFS has no native file-created notification invoking a Fargate service. C: S3 event -> Lambda dispatcher -> ECS Fargate is supported. D: Lambda container images do not remove the 15-minute timeout and cannot process two-hour jobs.
plainWords: Move uploads to S3, use Lambda to choose and launch the correct Fargate task, and process the file for up to two hours.
keyPoints: Lambda 15-minute maximum even for container images; Fargate handles long-running tasks; S3 ObjectCreated event can invoke Lambda; EFS lacks native per-file-created notifications.
sourceWarning: CRITICAL: Wrong source key D corrected to C. D exceeds Lambda maximum runtime. A/B assume nonexistent EFS file-create event notifications. Fixed punctuation and OCR spacing. External sites reproduce single-answer question; no verified Choose TWO/THREE variant.

review.notes: Domain 4 93/139; 2-hour task exceeds Lambda maximum. Answer corrected D to C. No verified multi-answer variant.

stem: A company migrated an application from on-premises VMs to Amazon EC2 instances in an AWS account 6 months ago. Now, the company needs to deploy the application to a second AWS Region. During the next 2 years, the company will redesign parts of the application to use AWS Lambda functions. The company is expecting stable usage patterns for the application for the next 3 years. Which strategy will MAXIMIZE the cost savings for the company?

options.text: Evaluate Savings Plans recommendations each year in AWS Cost Management. Purchase a 1-year Compute Savings Plan based on the recommendations.

Evaluate Savings Plans recommendations by using AWS Compute Optimizer. Purchase a 3-year EC2 Instance Savings Plan based on the recommendations. Use Compute Optimizer to adjust the Lambda functions based on recommendations.

Purchase a 1-year EC2 Instance Savings Plan with No Upfront payment. Review the infrastructure after each year. As parts of the application transition to Lambda functions, decrease the hourly commitment for future EC2 Instance Savings Plans.
Purchase a 3-year EC2 Instance Savings Plan with No Upfront payment. As parts of the application transition to Lambda functions, decrease the hourly commitment for the EC2 Instance Savings Plan.

explanation: A is the best answer among the choices. Compute Savings Plans apply to eligible EC2 usage across instance families and AWS Regions and also to Lambda (and Fargate), so they remain usable as workloads expand to another Region and migrate from EC2 to Lambda. One-year commitments let the company re-evaluate its required hourly spend each year using AWS Cost Management/Cost Explorer Savings Plans recommendations. A three-year plan may provide a higher percentage discount on stable eligible usage, but none of the offered three-year options covers Lambda or has equivalent Region/family flexibility.
wrongOptionsExplanation: A: Correct: 1-year Compute Savings Plans retain cross-Region and EC2-to-Lambda flexibility with annual commitment resizing. B: Incorrect: EC2 Instance Savings Plans apply only to a specified EC2 instance family in a Region, not Lambda, and a 3-year term increases lock-in; AWS Cost Explorer is the primary Savings Plans recommendation interface. C: Incorrect: Future EC2 Instance Savings Plans can be bought with smaller commitments, but they still do not cover Lambda or move freely across Regions/families; No Upfront does not mean adjustable commitment. D: Incorrect: Existing 3-year EC2 Instance Savings Plans commitments cannot be reduced as EC2 is replaced by Lambda, and do not cover Lambda.
plainWords: Choose a one-year Compute Savings Plan, review AWS Cost Explorer recommendations annually, and renew at a commitment that fits the evolving EC2 and Lambda mix across Regions.
keyPoints: Compute Savings Plans cover EC2, Fargate and Lambda across Regions and instance families. EC2 Instance Savings Plans cover a selected instance family in one Region, not Lambda. Savings Plans commitments cannot be decreased during their term. No Upfront affects payment timing, not flexibility. One-year terms trade maximum discount for flexibility. 'MAXIMIZE' is not provable numerically without spend projections.
sourceWarning: MINOR QUALIFICATION: The wording 'MAXIMIZE cost savings' cannot be mathematically established without usage and prices; 3-year Compute Savings Plans (not offered) could yield higher discounts on predictable baseline spend. Among supplied choices A best fits multi-Region and EC2-to-Lambda migration. Exact-stem FreeCram version is a four-option single-answer question. No confirmed Choose TWO/THREE variant.

review.notes: Domain 4 94/139. Correct A. AWS confirms Compute SP applies across Regions and EC2/Lambda. Existing commitments fixed. Exact-stem FreeCram single-answer version; no verified Choose TWO/THREE variant. Maximize cannot be guaranteed without cost modeling.

stem: A company is running an application on Amazon EC2 instances in the AWS Cloud. The application is using a MongoDB database with a replica set as its data tier. The MongoDB database is installed on systems in the company's on-premises data center and is accessible through an AWS Direct Connect connection to the data center environment. A solutions architect must migrate the on-premises MongoDB database to Amazon DocumentDB (with MongoDB compatibility). Which strategy should the solutions architect choose to perform this migration?

options.text: Create a fleet of EC2 instances. Install MongoDB Community Edition on the EC2 instances, and create a database. Configure continuous synchronous replication with the database that is running in the on-premises data center.

Create an AWS Database Migration Service (AWS DMS) replication instance. Create a source endpoint for the on-premises MongoDB database by using change data capture (CDC). Create a target endpoint for the Amazon DocumentDB database. Create and run a DMS migration task.

Create a data migration pipeline by using AWS Data Pipeline. Define data nodes for the on-premises MongoDB database and the Amazon DocumentDB database. Create a scheduled task to run the data pipeline.

Create a source endpoint for the on-premises MongoDB database by using AWS Glue crawlers. Configure continuous asynchronous replication between the MongoDB database and the Amazon DocumentDB database.

explanation: B is correct. AWS DMS supports a self-managed on-premises MongoDB replica set as a source and Amazon DocumentDB as a target. Configure the MongoDB source endpoint and DocumentDB target endpoint, use Document mode, and create a full-load-and-CDC task for initial data plus ongoing changes. DMS requires access to MongoDB's replica-set oplog/change stream for CDC, sufficient oplog retention, and network/TLS permissions through Direct Connect. Validate the load and replication lag before cutover. AWS also offers newer homogeneous DMS migration options, but B is the only supported option among the listed choices.
wrongOptionsExplanation: A: Incorrect: Deploys another self-managed MongoDB database on EC2 instead of migrating to managed DocumentDB; synchronous replication as proposed is not a DocumentDB migration strategy. B: Correct: DMS replication instance with MongoDB CDC source and DocumentDB target enables full load plus ongoing replication. C: Incorrect: AWS Data Pipeline is a scheduled workflow orchestration service, not native MongoDB CDC replication; it stopped accepting new customers July 25, 2025. D: Incorrect: AWS Glue crawlers discover schemas/metadata; they do not create DMS-style MongoDB source endpoints or continuous MongoDB-to-DocumentDB replication.
plainWords: Use AWS DMS to copy MongoDB data to DocumentDB, keep changes synchronized through CDC, then switch the application over.
keyPoints: MongoDB replica set provides oplog/change stream for DMS CDC; size oplog for full-load duration (AWS recommends 24h retention). Use Document mode for DocumentDB target. Set full load + CDC for initial and incremental migration. Direct Connect provides private connectivity, not migration by itself. AWS Data Pipeline closed to new customers July 25, 2025.
sourceWarning: MINOR OMISSION: Option B mentions a CDC source endpoint but does not explicitly say to select full load + CDC for existing data; ensure the DMS task includes initial full load as well as ongoing replication. DMS also supports newer homogeneous serverless migrations, but replication-instance option remains valid. Option C is additionally outdated because AWS Data Pipeline stopped accepting new customers July 25, 2025. Exact-stem external sources FreeCram and CertsMania both key B as single-answer; no verified Choose TWO/THREE variant.

review.notes: Domain 4 95/139. Confirmed B via AWS MongoDB source/DocumentDB target and two external exact-stem single-answer copies. No confirmed Choose TWO/THREE variant. Flag initial full load + CDC omission and Data Pipeline July 2025 new-customer closure.
